item.title: Corporate Social Responsibility in Times of Societal Polarization, Politicization, and Securitization
item.content:encoded:
Dorothee Maria Winkler, Bern University of Applied Sciences

David Risi, Bern University of Applied Sciences

Christopher Wickert, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

Onna Malou van den Broek, Copenhagen Business School

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has a long and influential history as one of the dominant paradigms in managing the business-society interface. For years, CSR has served as the normative and strategic blueprint for companies in managing growing societal expectations such as climate change, corruption, and inequality, fundamentally shaping corporate behavior across sustainability, ethics, and stakeholder engagement. Over the past decade, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria seemed to be moving from the periphery to the center of attention for companies, and the formalization and legalization of CSR-related criteria have reinforced the importance of corporate responsibility and consolidated its position as a central area of concern for business firms.

However, after a long period of broad consensus on the desirability of business responsibility, the global political, social, and economic landscape has shifted in ways that fundamentally challenge the taken-for-granted position of CSR and related ideas about the role of business in society. These shifts occur amid widespread societal polarization, in which democratic countries face a profound sociocultural struggle between contending conservative and progressive visions, contributing to the erosion of democratic norms. We observe an active dismantling of CSR alongside the contraction and de-institutionalization of moral markets. As a result, CSR and sustainability have become highly polarized, reflecting broader political conflicts over the role of business in society.

The consequences of these developments are visible in corporate behavior. Businesses have begun to withdraw from seemingly firm commitments to sustainability and are recalibrating their strategies and operational activities. Leading firms, including major U.S. Big Tech companies such as Meta and Amazon, have rolled back or abandoned diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives almost overnight, potentially to align with shifting political priorities. U.S. firms increasingly adopt a reverse CSR approach, curtailing DEI efforts to appease political leadership or engaging in symbolic acts of proximity to power. Concepts such as "greenhushing"—the deliberate under-communication of CSR activities to avoid public and political attention—are once again becoming more important.

Overall, we witness the rise of populist and nationalist movements across Western democracies that eroded the political consensus and Zeitgeist supporting corporate responsibility frameworks. Alongside polarization, geopolitical tensions such as the persistence of violent conflicts like the Russia-Ukraine war and the escalation of competition among major economic and political powers have shifted state and corporate priorities away from shared responsibility toward national interests and security concerns. For instance, in November 2025, the European Parliament voted to substantially weaken corporate sustainability rules and green investments, exempting over 80% of companies from due diligence requirements, in favor of rearmament and economic competitiveness priorities.

This trend has redefined sustainability itself. ESG funds that once excluded weapon manufacturers on ethical grounds are now promoting "defense funds" framed around protecting freedom and democracy. Similarly, the British government has encouraged private investors to reassess defense as a positive ESG category. Overall, rising polarization, particularly in Europe following the Russia-Ukraine war as well as the Israel-U.S.-Iran war, has enabled political and business actors to reshape CSR and ESG frameworks to morally legitimize investments in the arms industry, long regarded as a "sin industry" and excluded by sustainable investors.

The instrumentalization of CSR for political purposes is not a new phenomenon. In autocratic contexts such as China or in many African countries, CSR has often been used to strengthen governmental relations and fulfill political rather than social objectives. What is new is the growing reconceptualization of CSR in democratic contexts to serve national and geopolitical interests rather than universal social or environmental goals as well as the concern that elites in these countries have been more accepting of autocratization and democratic backsliding to serve geopolitical interests.

The consequence of these developments is that the intersection and repercussions of societal polarization, politicization, and securitization are fragmenting CSR itself: its overall meaning and scope, its broader role in guiding business's place in society, and the way CSR is being strategized and operationalized by business firms. As corporations realign around national interests rather than universal norms, CSR is becoming more diverse and context-specific, leading to divergent approaches shaped by geopolitical and domestic political factors. These emerging CSR models remain poorly understood. Against this backdrop, this special issue is guided by the overarching question: What does Corporate Social Responsibility entail in times of societal polarization, politicization, and securitization?

Potential topics

  • What responsibilities do firms assume when navigating heightened political and societal tensions?
  • What does "responsible" corporate behavior mean in today's polarized global political economy?
  • How is CSR evolving to address the complex moral and strategic challenges of an increasingly divided world?
  • Do corporations counter populist and illiberal politics, or primarily align with dominant power structures?
  • How do firms recalibrate ESG and CSR commitments while maintaining legitimacy across diverse stakeholders?
  • Which role does CSR play in specific industries such as defense industrial complex, including defense-focused tech firms?
  • To what extent has CSR enabled corporate political activity (CPA) that influences democratic governance in ways that advance corporate interests?
  • How do new forms of "reverse CSR" or politically adaptive responsibility emerge?
  • How does the geographical context influence the conceptualization of CSR?
  • Is CSR diffusing from autocratic to democratic contexts as a tool of political signaling rather than social progress?
  • How do the underlying philosophical and epistemological assumptions of CSR differ across contexts?
  • How can established theoretical perspectives account for geopolitically fragmented CSR models?
  • How can nationalistic or "Western populist" CSR be conceptualized in a priori democratic contexts?
  • What theoretical frameworks need to be developed to account for the instrumentalization of CSR for national and geopolitical purposes?
  • Which role does CSR play in contexts of violent conflict?
  • How do security demands shape CSR's definition and scope?
  • What new priorities emerge when CSR is applied in the defense industry, particularly regarding process vs. product dimensions?
  • How do polarization, politicization, and securitization collectively shape CSR trajectories, and what role do businesses, governments, and other stakeholders play?
  • How do businesses weigh and prioritize imperatives posed by polarization, politicization, and securitization, and how does this influence their CSR agendas?
  • How do businesses recalibrate their CSR strategies to account for new and competing societal priorities?
  • How do governments integrate these dynamics when devising or revising CSR regulations?
  • Do we see emerging surveillance states arising from mutually beneficial collaborations between the defense-industrial complex (including tech firms) and governments?
  • Do we observe any sidelining or dismantling of international institutions and cooperation structures established after the Second World War?
  • How do societal stakeholders navigate this nexus when formulating expectations towards businesses and exerting pressure?

Timeline

  • September 1, 2026: Deadline for extended abstract submission for paper development workshop
  • October 5, 2026: Online pre-submission workshop (participation optional)
  • August 1, 2027: Submission window opens
  • August 31, 2027: Submission window closes

item.title: The Startup Workforce
item.content:encoded:
James Bort, DePaul University

Veroniek Collewaert, Vlerick Business School

Yuval Engel, University of Amsterdam

Evy Van Lancker, Ghent University

Johan Wiklund, Syracuse University

The startup workforce represents a distinct and consequential stakeholder in entrepreneurship that has been systematically understudied relative to founders and funders. Early insights from the Stanford Project on Emerging Companies revealed how organizational changes within startups disproportionately impacted long-tenured employees. This pioneering work laid the foundation for understanding how startups differ from established firms in their approach to human capital, including fundamental aspects such as compensation, staffing, and performance management.

Contemporary research has deepened our understanding of the unique dynamics between startups and their employees. Whereas early research identified demographic patterns, illustrating that startup employees tend to be younger and risk-tolerant, recent work has uncovered more nuanced dynamics. For example, experienced employees often join startups when they have partners with stable careers, but can also command wage premiums as firms grow. Startup employees are drawn in by passionate founders, opportunities for greater freedom and responsibility, and the potential for significant financial upside.

Startups have a limited reputation as an employer which makes recruiting a challenge; however, there is evidence that talented individuals prefer startups in some contexts. As such, startups tend to recruit through previous affiliations and when proximal, these relationships can increase firm performance. Despite the allure of building a startup alongside founders and crafting unique roles, nascent firms have specific recruitment challenges and are generally more challenging places to work.

Startups tend to have underdeveloped human resources functions, leading to managerial and socio-structural challenges that ultimately trickle down to the employee. Scaling a startup's operations is difficult, and employees' growing pains are difficult to suppress during times of rapid expansion, leading to the accumulation of various forms of organizational 'debt' as the costs of growth outweigh the startup's ability to absorb them.

In sum, the startup context challenges traditional assumptions about employee-organization relationships, demanding new theoretical frameworks that can advance both entrepreneurship and organizational scholarship.

For the purposes of this special issue, the startup workforce is defined as the non-founding individuals who contribute labor to the creation and development of an early-stage venture. This workforce includes, but is not limited to, those under formal employment. As such, the workforce also encompasses contractors, fractional executives, agencies, platform and ghost workers, and other non-standard labor that contributes to venture creation alongside payrolled employees. It is, however, distinct from founders and external stakeholders who do not work inside the venture. In practice, the boundary between the earliest employees and founders may be fuzzy, and contributions that interrogate how this boundary is drawn, contested, and made consequential are welcomed.

The special issue approaches the startup workforce as a relational phenomenon rather than a static population of employees inside a firm, one that spans individuals, firms, and the institutional environments in which startups are embedded. This framing invites contributions that take power, voice, and regulation seriously, and that use the distinctiveness of the startup context to export ideas back to adjacent fields.

This special issue aims to advance understanding of the startup workforce by bringing together researchers from fields such as entrepreneurship, organizational behavior, human resource management, economics, and sociology. Contributions from any disciplinary tradition are welcome, provided they engage substantively with the startup workforce. Theory borrowed from adjacent fields is welcome when it does genuine explanatory work for startup workforce phenomena; it is not welcome when it provides labels for statistical relationships without specifying the mechanisms through which those relationships operate in the entrepreneurial context.

Consistent with the journal's editorial direction, submissions are evaluated on the alignment between research question, research design, and data quality. An important research question about the startup workforce, paired with a design capable of answering it and data of sufficient quality to support credible conclusions, matters more than theoretical novelty or conceptual sophistication. The journal values work that not only explains mechanisms but also clarifies what the evidence means for the choices founders, employees, and investors face in practice.

Empirical papers that illuminate convincing causal mechanisms are highly encouraged, whether through quasi-experimental designs, longitudinal panel studies, field experiments, qualitative process tracing, ethnographies, or mixed-methods research. The journal is equally receptive to computational approaches and studies that leverage novel data sources: linked employer-employee datasets, platform data, administrative records, and other unconventional sources can open windows into startup employment dynamics. Multi-method approaches that triangulate findings across different research designs are especially valued.

For studies relying on distal sources such as archival or census data, authors are expected to demonstrate how the theorized mechanisms are reflected in the measurement architecture, not merely inferred. Data quality is evaluated by fitness-for-purpose rather than by representativeness alone, and work that invests in novel infrastructure and integrates multimodal sources is welcomed. Designs that exploit exogenous variation in the policy environment of startup employment, such as changes in non-compete enforcement, worker classification rules, equity-compensation taxation, or visa regimes, to identify causal effects on recruitment, retention, mobility, and venture outcomes are particularly welcome.

Given the nested nature of the startup workforce, multi-level theoretical approaches and research designs are appreciated; the interplay among individual employees, founder-employee dyads, teams, organizations, and broader labor markets represents fertile ground for contributions that capture the complexity of startup employment. Studies that pre-register hypotheses, share replication materials, or otherwise embrace open-science principles are valued and will be recognized during the review process. Direct and conceptual replications, robustness and multiverse analyses, informative null findings, and Registered Reports-style submissions with pre-reviewed designs are welcomed.

The rapid development of AI-based tools has fundamentally changed what it means to produce a conceptual contribution. Purely review-oriented papers and conceptual pieces that primarily synthesize existing ideas without empirical grounding are less likely to be competitive; however, field-defining theoretical contributions that advance understanding beyond what existing work has established will be considered.

Potential topics

  • Employee motivations and retention across venture stages
  • Recruitment, employer branding, and the role of prior affiliations in startup hiring
  • The influence of early employees on organizational culture, routines, and strategic direction
  • Compensation structures, equity arrangements, and evolving psychological contracts
  • Workforce well-being, occupational stress, and founder-employee emotional spillovers
  • The impact of hybrid and remote work on startup employment dynamics
  • The opportunities and adversity of AI in light of startup employment and work ethic, and workforce diversity, inclusion, and the role of HR professionalization in early-stage ventures
  • Worker voice, collective action, and power asymmetries in startups, including unionization, whistleblowing, hustle culture and exploitation, equity and vesting disputes, and the dark side of founder–employee relations
  • The regulatory and institutional environment of startup employment, including non-compete enforcement, worker classification, equity taxation, and visa regimes
  • Non-standard and hybrid labor forms, including contractors, fractional executives, agencies, platform and ghost work, and globally distributed teams
  • Post-startup career trajectories, including employee mobility, alumni networks, and entrepreneurial spawning after exit, acquisition, or failure
  • The scaleup transition and its workforce implications, including when and how a startup workforce ceases to be one and how HR professionalization reshapes the employment relation
  • AI-native ventures as a new organizational form, where a small number of humans operate agentic systems and the category of workforce is itself reconstituted
  • Startup workforces outside North America and Western Europe, including emerging-economy, informal, and cross-border contexts

Timeline

  • Invalid DateTime: Academy of Management PDW
  • December 31, 2026: Extended abstracts due for participation in May workshop
  • May 1, 2027: Special issue editorial workshop for invited participants based on proposals (hosted in United States)
  • August 30, 2027: Full papers due for submission following second workshop
  • November 1, 2027: Special issue editorial workshop for invited participants based on full papers (hosted in Europe)
  • January 1, 2028: Full papers invited for submission
item.author: Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice (SAGE)

item.title: Reexamining and Replicating Foundational Studies in Entrepreneurship Research
item.content:encoded:
Karl Wennberg, Stockholm School of Economics

Jeremy C. Short, University of North Texas

Jeffrey A. Chandler, University of North Texas

Marcus Wolfe, University of North Texas

Sebastian Kruse, RWTH University

Carolin Krieweth, RWTH University

This Special Issue seeks to advance our understanding of replication in entrepreneurship research by encouraging rigorous reexaminations of foundational empirical studies. Replication is essential for cumulative theory development and for establishing confidence in empirical findings. In a dynamic field such as entrepreneurship, where institutional environments, technologies, funding regimes, and societal expectations evolve rapidly, systematic replication is particularly critical to assess whether foundational relationships reflect stable theoretical mechanisms or context-specific patterns.

Despite its importance, recent evidence suggests that entrepreneurship research has not yet developed a strong replication culture. A comprehensive review shows that replication efforts remain rare, fragmented, and skewed toward conceptual extensions and empirical generalizations, while exact replications, reanalyses of original data, and checking-of-analysis designs are comparatively scarce. Moreover, many of the field's most influential empirical studies, particularly those published in leading journals and widely cited, have either never been replicated or have been replicated only once. As a result, widely cited findings continue to shape theoretical debates and inform practice without systematic assessment of their robustness, temporal stability, or boundary conditions.

This Special Issue calls for rigorous, theory-driven replication studies that revisit foundational relationships and contribute to a more robust and context-sensitive understanding of entrepreneurship phenomena. Replication is not viewed merely as a confirmation exercise but as a critical tool for theory refinement, extension, and adjudication between competing explanations. Submissions employing diverse methodological approaches are welcome, provided they are theoretically grounded and methodologically rigorous. Multi-study designs that combine exact replication or reanalysis of original data with subsequent empirical generalization or theoretical extension are particularly encouraged, as such designs can offer deeper insights into when, how, and why established findings hold or vary across contexts.

All manuscripts will be subject to the journal's standard double-blind review process and must meet the publication standards of Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Submissions will be assessed based on their theoretical contribution, methodological rigor, and their ability to advance cumulative theory development in entrepreneurship, rather than on whether findings confirm prior results.

The guest editors will organize a series of paper development workshops (PDWs) aligned with the theme of the Special Issue prior to the submission deadline. The in-person workshop will take place at the University of North Texas in late February 2027, complemented by a virtual workshop in early March 2027. The PDWs are designed to support authors in developing rigorous, theory-driven replication studies, with particular encouragement for multi-study designs. Participation is entirely voluntary and is not a prerequisite for submission or consideration in the review process.

Potential topics

  • The 33 most cited entrepreneurship studies (each exceeding 1,000 citations) identified as priority candidates for replication
  • Influential studies within specific BCERC research tracks highlighted as influential contributions within each track
  • Studies with credible cases for broader influence on entrepreneurship research
  • Identifying boundary conditions and contextual contingencies of established relationships
  • Clarifying inconsistencies or mixed findings in prior research
  • Refining theoretical mechanisms underlying key constructs and relationships
  • Contributing to methodological transparency, rigor, and best practices in replication research
  • Multi-study designs combining exact replication or reanalysis of original data with subsequent empirical generalization or theoretical extension

Timeline

  • December 1, 2026: Deadline for short proposal submission for paper development workshop participation (3,000-5,000 words)
  • February 1, 2027: In-person paper development workshop at University of North Texas
  • March 1, 2027: Virtual paper development workshop
  • May 1, 2027: Manuscript submission window opens
  • August 1, 2027: Manuscript submission deadline (midnight U.S. Eastern Time)

item.title: Family Firms as Context for Organizational Behavior Processes
item.content:encoded:
Melanie De Ruiter, Nyenrode Business University

Benjamin D. McLarty, Louisiana Tech University

Denise M. Rousseau, Carnegie Mellon University

James M. Vardaman, Memphis University

Despite calls to consider context in Organizational Behavior (OB) and management research, the broader OB and management literature has largely ignored family firms and the experiences and employment dynamics of their employees. OB research samples often are drawn without considering the nature of the settings involved or any potential impact on the variables of interest. Since family firms are a common type of business, ranging from sixty-five to ninety percent worldwide, samples in many OB and management studies likely conflate respondents from family and non-family firms. Such conflation can mask differences in behavioral processes that can result in erroneous inferences.

Treatment of family/non-family business as a dichotomous moderator only allows general differences to be noted without theoretically comparing psychological processes at the individual, team, and organizational levels. Moreover, since there is considerable heterogeneity within family firms, grouping employees working in different family firms together will likely forego important across family firm contextual differences in OB processes. Most studies in family firm research have been described as 'context-less'.

This special issue focuses on micro-OB processes in family firms, with the aim of extending recent endeavors on contextualizing family firm research by specifically focusing on the psychological and behavioral processes occurring within the family firm. Special attention is drawn to non-family employees in family firms, a prevalent group within the global workforce but surprisingly under-researched.

The special issue seeks answers to the questions: 'How do micro-OB concepts, processes and theories play out in family firm settings?', 'Why do micro-OB concepts, processes and theories play out in family firms in a particular way?' and 'How can an in-depth understanding of family firm phenomena extend knowledge or offer unique insights about micro-OB concepts, processes and theories?'. OB processes and outcomes that occur in family businesses are likely to be different from those found in non-family firms, yet family firm research is dominated by economic, financial and socio-economic frameworks often with little attention to OB-related phenomena.

To shed light on OB processes in family firms, scholars need theories of context to better specify OB dynamics characterizing family firms at the individual, team, and organizational levels and to compare these across family firms and to other kinds of firms. Scholars debate whether family firms are worse or better employers, with some arguing they are more conflict-filled because the goals of family and business systems may be at odds. However, informative contextual comparisons are largely lacking.

Articles should focus on meaningful theorizing about context and contextual differences in OB processes. Articles that focus on dichotomous family/non-family firm comparisons or simply conduct a study within a family firm without meaningful theorizing about context are not considered. Rather, articles should directly capture context through specific assessments to test measurement invariance and in-depth comparison of contextual differences, drawing from theories of context. The special issue welcomes data-based research articles, conceptual papers, reviews and critiques of research, and encourages qualitative research approaches for exploring emic concepts and heterogeneity within family firms.

Potential topics

  • Development and validation of measurement instruments (including assessment of measurement invariance) that allow a more generic assessment of contextual effects often put forward in family firm research (e.g., socioemotional wealth) to help theorize and understand similarities and differences in OB processes between family and non-family firms, and within family firms
  • Explicit tests of theories of context (e.g., trait activation theory; situation strength theory) to explain differences in relationships between personality traits and employee outcomes between family and non-family firms and within different types of family firms (e.g., enhanced understanding of family firm context as a driver for personality activation and impact on workplace performance and behaviors)
  • Development and validation of personality measurement instruments specific to the context of family for use in family firms, and meaningful contextual comparisons across family firms (including assessment of measurement invariance)
  • Enhanced theoretical understanding of how bifurcation bias based on family firm context as a potential motivational force for driving employee attitudes and behaviors
  • Multilevel research to better understand how the family firm context affects the extent to which leadership styles may (or may not) trickle down from family executives to family and non-family managers and in turn affect non-family employee outcomes in different types of family firms
  • An exploration of how critical events within the family firm context and family/non-family member dynamics shape employee and non-family manager perceptions and evaluations of their employment relationship with the family firm

Timeline

  • December 15, 2025: Proposal submission deadline
  • February 15, 2026: Decisions and feedback on proposals
  • February 1, 2027: Full manuscript submission deadline
  • May 1, 2027: Decisions and reviews on manuscripts
  • August 1, 2027: Revised manuscripts due
  • November 1, 2027: Second round decisions and reviews on revised manuscripts
  • February 1, 2028: Second round revised manuscripts due
  • April 1, 2028: SI editorial final review round and decisions on revised manuscripts
  • May 15, 2028: Final submissions of manuscripts
  • June 1, 2028: Final decision by guest editors
  • July 1, 2028: Accepted manuscripts to publisher

item.title: Advancing Management Research Through Theory Testing: A Special Issue of Replication and Reproducibility Studies
item.content:encoded:
William G. Obenauer, University of Maine

Robyn L. Brouer, University of South Alabama

Rachel Clapp-Smith, University of North Georgia

Ajay Rama Ponnapalli, Wayne State University

Andreas Schwab, Iowa State University

Jost Sieweke, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

Chen Wang, Western Michigan University

Group & Organizational Management (GOM) has made an explicit commitment to publishing replication research and contributing to an ecosystem that supports replication research in the organizational sciences. By making this commitment, GOM joins journals such as Strategic Management Journal, The Leadership Quarterly, Entrepreneurship: Theory and Practice, and Journal of Management Scientific Reports in this endeavor.

As part of GOM's commitment to supporting replication research, this special issue aims to stimulate a continued stream of replication and reproducibility submissions to GOM well beyond the publication of this special issue. Focal studies (i.e., studies replicated or reproduced) are not required to have been published in GOM, but they should be of interest to GOM's audience.

The special issue welcomes three types of submissions. Registered reports require researchers to submit their introduction and methods description before collecting data and will include detailed descriptions for either literal replication, literal reproducibility studies, or multi-study replication papers. Registered reports must include all methodological details as reviewers cannot grant acceptance in principle when methods lack transparency. Authors are encouraged to submit registered reports at least four months before the submission deadline to allow time for data collection. Importantly, authors must not collect data before their action editor gives acceptance in principle.

Literal replication or reproducibility study only submissions are limited to 2,000 words with limited introductions and discussion sections, with the majority of text focused on methodology and results. This recognizes the importance of bolstering the research record through literal replication and literal reproducibility studies.

Full-length submissions should use conceptual or constructive replication to advance knowledge through boundary testing or methodological improvements. Authors are encouraged to include reproducibility studies and/or literal replications within their full-length submissions for benchmarking purposes. While conducting a literal replication before constructive replication is encouraged, it is not required, as conducting reproducibility studies or literal replications may sometimes be infeasible due to practical constraints such as limited access to samples.

Potential topics

  • Registered reports on literal replications, literal reproducibility studies, or multi-study replication designs
  • Literal replication and reproducibility studies (single-study submissions)
  • Full-length submissions using conceptual or constructive replication to advance knowledge through boundary testing or methodological improvements
  • Reproducibility studies and literal replications for benchmarking purposes within full-length submissions
  • Replication research advancing organizational sciences

Timeline

  • June 30, 2027: Initial Submissions Due

This special issue seeks to explore the multifaceted ways in which political environments shape and influence the tourism and hospitality sectors. The political context encompasses governmental policies, political stability, regulatory frameworks, international relations, and geopolitical events that directly and indirectly affect tourism flows, hospitality operations, and industry development.

We invite submissions that examine how political factors influence destination competitiveness, tourism demand and supply, hospitality business strategies, employment patterns, and sustainable development in the sector. Contributions may include empirical studies, theoretical frameworks, case studies, and comparative analyses that provide insights into the complex relationships between political environments and tourism and hospitality industries globally.

item.title: AI-Enabled Experience Innovation
item.content:encoded:
Bernd Schmitt, Columbia University

Ming-Hui Huang, National Taiwan University

Sanjay Sood, University of California, Los Angeles

Shuyi Hao, ICN Business School

AI is innovating how service experiences can be designed, curated, and delivered. Service that emphasizes experiential components, such as sensory, affective, cognitive, behavioral and social elements, are considered experiential service. Customer experience is multidimensional across multiple touchpoints, unfolds over the customer journey, can be enabled by various AI technologies, and can establish emotional connections with customers.

This special issue seeks to advance our understanding of how AI can enable experience innovation. By enabling personalization, adaptive interaction, and multisensory engagement, AI allows service providers to create new, innovative experiences and enables customers to participate in journeys that evolve dynamically with their needs and preferences. For examples, augmented and virtual reality technologies (AR/VR) are used in retailing to innovate experiences; extended-reality technologies (XR) are used to bring static museum exhibitions to life, mixed-reality technologies (MR) are used to blend real and virtual skill development, and AI technologies are used to enhance sports or entertainment experiences through digital images and surround sound.

The special issue welcomes submissions from all disciplines with a service interest, such as consumer research, service marketing, strategic management, information systems, operations research, psychology, and sociology. Mixed methods blending conceptual, empirical, or computational approaches are encouraged.

Papers will undergo no more than two rounds of full peer review. After the second round, a final decision will be made to ensure timely publication. The special issue operates on a tight timeline, and authors should expect quick turnarounds for reviews and revisions.

Potential topics

  • How do AI technologies (e.g., generative AI, agentic AI, AR, VR, XR, MR) innovate service experiences, and what design principles help service providers create engaging and meaningful experiences?
  • How should AI-enabled experiences be orchestrated across physical, digital, and extended-reality touchpoints throughout the service journey?
  • How can service providers create and scale AI-enabled experience innovations for human customers, hybrid human-AI customers, or autonomous AI customers to generate favorable outcomes for customers, providers, and ecosystems?
  • What new experiential consequences and innovation outcomes arise from AI, and how can they be conceptualized, measured, and managed over time?
  • What ethical, societal, or governance challenges arise and how can AI-enabled experience innovation be designed, governed, and managed responsibly?

Timeline

  • August 1, 2026: Submission window opens
  • September 3, 2026: Full papers due
  • September 30, 2026: Submissions close
  • August 1, 2027: Special issue planned publication
item.author: Journal of Service Research (SAGE)

item.title: Immanent Critique in Management Learning and Education: Organizational Contradictions, Emancipatory Possibilities, and Institutional Transformation
item.content:encoded:
Torkild Thanem, Stockholm University

Shoaib Ul Haq, University of Greenwich

Sara Zaeemdar, Newcastle University

Iain Munro, Newcastle University

Alice Wickström, Aalto University

Farooq Mughal, University of Bath

This special issue addresses an underexplored concern in Management Learning and Education (MLE): the contradictions between the emancipatory ideals espoused by business schools and the institutional, ideological and economic logics they reproduce. Critics have charged MLE with neoliberal, colonial, racist, and sexist practices, which reproduce the harms and injustices of capitalism. However important such work is, these critiques have largely been mounted from a position external to the institutions they target. Less examined is how transformation may be pursued from inside MLE itself, by holding business schools accountable to the very ideals they profess.

The tension is fundamental. Business schools operate as market-driven enterprises while proclaiming educational missions centred on ethics, sustainability, and social responsibility. They continue to train the architects and lackeys of an economic system breaching planetary boundaries while housing sustainability modules that rarely examine the growth imperative running through the wider curriculum. But even though the gap between ecological pedagogy and the ecological consequences of business-as-usual education has become a defining contradiction of the field, such instability also opens space for reimagining the purpose and practice of management education. Institutions that fail to do so risk obsolescence, with their academic freedom further eroded by political intervention or being outdone by AI tools that beat them at their own game of dubious knowledge creation.

Immanent critique offers a particularly valuable method to work through these contradictions and the transformational possibilities that they harbour. In essence, immanent critique combines internal critique with normative critique. Whereas internal critique involves thorough empirical analysis to identify dissonance between institutional claims and reality, normative critique appeals to standards reconstructed from, or held up against, the institution itself. This dual approach lets scholars identify discrepancies between stated missions and operational realities while judging institutions against broader standards of justice and sustainability. Unlike external critique, which imposes outside standards, or ideology critique, which assumes that participants are deluded by false consciousness, immanent critique examines institutions from the inside.

Two things complicate the exercise of immanent critique in business schools. Firstly, business schools speak polyvocally through voices that often pull in opposing directions (through accreditation regimes, faculty research cultures, student demands, donor expectations, etc.). As a result, immanent critique in MLE is no neutral mirroring of declared values but requires careful reconstruction of institutional normativity. Secondly, immanent critique involves the everyday practices of faculty, students, and staff without being confined to the classroom. Such praxis may be enacted on the margins of business schools, through climate occupations and divestment campaigns, anti-war encampments, decolonial reading groups, sanctuary classrooms, strike action and curricular sabotage. Used this way, immanent critique offers a way of revitalising MLE not by indicting it from outside but by internal engagement for institutional transformation.

Working through the internal and external contradictions of business schools, immanent critique turns tensions into pedagogical resources. When business schools claim to educate ethical leaders while prioritising profit maximisation, students can examine organisational hypocrisy not simply as the moral failure of individuals but as structural contradictions requiring systemic solutions. Historical precedent supports this approach: business schools themselves were born of contradictions between professional training and academic legitimacy; contradictions between theory and practice gave way to innovations such as the case method and interdisciplinary curricula. Although these transformations were neither uncontested nor unequivocally emancipatory, they do point to the capacity of MLE to be reconstituted through, rather than against, its internal tensions. Today's challenges call for a similarly fundamental reimagining of purpose and pedagogy.

Methodologically, immanent critique can be pursued through a plurality of approaches. Ethnography is well suited to surfacing contradictions between what people say and what they do, but historical and archival analysis, textual and discursive reconstruction, participatory action research, philosophical reconstruction of institutional norms, and arts-based inquiry are equally legitimate paths into the same problem. By centring the experiences of those inside MLE, immanent critique builds theory from practice and helps close the theory-practice divide in critical management research. The empirical exposition of institutional contradictions also facilitates critique-in-use, that is, forms of critical practice that enable emancipatory change by collectively creating the conditions in which new thinking and new forms of organising may emerge.

Potential topics

  • Theoretical contributions developing immanent critique for MLE contexts
  • Scholarship examining how management education's contradictions relate to broader transformations in capitalism, knowledge production, and subjectivity formation
  • Efforts to rework immanent critique through decolonial, indigenous, and/or feminist epistemologies to address its Western/male-dominated philosophical origins
  • Efforts to develop conceptual frameworks for understanding emancipatory learning within constrained institutional contexts
  • Analyses of how business school commitments to sustainability, EDI, or social responsibility play out in curricular design, pedagogical practice, and institutional governance
  • Ethnographic investigations of alternative management education programs that attempt to embody different values while operating within conventional accreditation and funding structures
  • Studies of alternative institutional forms of management learning, such as cooperatives, free universities, worker-owned schools, platform-cooperative training programs, indigenous-led and faith-based business education
  • Critical investigations of the effects of the rise of far-right political leaders on progressive initiatives in education, such as EDI initiatives, equal pay and promotions, sustainability and ESG measures, and campus protests
  • Participatory research approaches that engage educators and learners as co-researchers in identifying and addressing educational contradictions
  • Arts-based methods for surfacing and representing the affective dimensions of educational contradictions and their role in reproducing or challenging institutional norms
  • Digital ethnographies examining online management education platforms and their claims versus experiences
  • Studies of the pedagogy of growth taught alongside curricula on planetary boundaries, ecological economics, and post-growth alternatives
  • Analyses of sustainability and ESG modules as moments of managerial absorption rather than ecological reckoning
  • Engagements with climate-justice movements as sources of immanent normative reconstruction inside the business school

Timeline

  • January 31, 2027: Submission of extended abstracts for the PDW
  • March 1, 2027: On-line PDW
  • August 15, 2027: Papers may be submitted electronically
  • September 15, 2027: Paper submission deadline

item.title: Organizing within the Planetary Boundaries
item.content:encoded:
Steve Kennedy, Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University

Brooke Lahneman, Montana State University

Lucrezia Nava, University of Exeter Business School

Amanda Williams, EM Lyon Business School

Scholarship on business sustainability increasingly views organizations as embedded within natural systems, conceptualized through the planetary boundaries framework. The planetary boundary framework defines nine Earth system processes that regulate the planet's stability and resilience and are directly affected by human activity. Alarmingly, seven of these nine boundaries have now been crossed, threatening both natural systems and the economies that depend on them. For business scholarship, this creates an urgent need to understand how organizations can operate and manage within the safe space delineated by planetary boundaries.

Much prior research on the natural environment in management has privileged firm-level outcomes such as financial performance and has overlooked the complex, coupled dynamics of ecological, social, and organizational systems. Drawing from ecology and biophysical system science, the planetary boundary framework provides both the conceptual and empirical depth to address this complexity and a scientifically grounded map of global limits to study how organizations affect — and are affected by — key ecological processes. It also serves as a boundary tool that enables interdisciplinary collaboration between management scholars and natural scientists.

Business scholars and practitioners increasingly recognize the need for deeper insight into sustainability that treats natural systems as operational and strategic constraints, as seen in rising attention to practical efforts such as the Science Based Targets Initiative to help companies align with planetary boundaries. However, integrating the planetary boundary framework into organizational research remains a challenge. One reason is that management research has largely been grounded in organization-focused theories and social science methodologies, with limited engagement with the natural sciences as a conceptual or empirical foundation. As a result, despite a growing body of work, a cohesive understanding of how the planetary boundary framework can bring the biophysical to the fore in organizational scholarship is still lacking.

This Special Issue responds to this gap by advancing the integration of the planetary boundary framework into management research and accelerating actionable insights into how organizations, their leaders, and the communities they affect can operate within planetary boundaries. The central question is: How can the planetary boundary framework be leveraged to develop theory and practice that illuminate the embeddedness of organizations within natural systems? Contributions should move beyond treating the natural environment as mere context, to position planetary boundaries as core organizing principles for theorizing, measuring, and guiding organizational action.

The Special Issue aims to spark scholarship that develops new concepts and empirical evidence grounded in biophysical system science; examines how organizations, industries, governments, and communities contribute to, or help avert, planetary boundary transgressions; and explores governance and innovation pathways that enable organizations to thrive while remaining within a safe and just operating space. The special issue sets out to push other boundaries too: the combined interdisciplinary networks of the guest editors allow drawing on natural scientists as readers, contributors, and reviewers to ensure reliable scientific evidence.

Both theoretical and empirical submissions from across business sustainability research are invited, with particular interest in studies that examine how organizations engage with biophysical limits and operate within the safe space defined by the planetary boundaries framework, leveraging planetary boundary concepts, models, or data to inform strategy, decision-making, and policy engagement. Studies investigating how organizations develop proactive and responsive strategies to address the interconnections between planetary boundaries and social issues, and studies that synthesize empirical insights from organizations and engage in forward-looking theorizing about how the planetary boundary framework could reshape organizing are welcome.

Research that emerges from collaboration with natural scientists or applies natural science methods and measures such as geospatial data, biodiversity and genetic diversity indicators is especially encouraged. While management research has focused heavily on climate change, papers addressing the other eight planetary boundaries are particularly welcome, including biosphere integrity, freshwater change, land-system change, biogeochemical flows, ocean acidification, stratospheric ozone depletion, atmospheric aerosol loading, and novel entities.

Potential topics

  • How Organizations Integrate the Planetary Boundary Framework into Strategy and Action
  • How organizations leverage planetary boundaries to inform sustainability materiality assessments and sustainability strategies
  • How organizations collectively use planetary boundaries as a basis to inform shared understanding of cross-scale risks across space and time
  • How organizations leverage planetary boundaries to inform risk management approaches
  • How organizations collectively build adaptive capacity for addressing risks and identifying opportunities associated with the planetary boundary framework
  • How organizations utilize planetary boundaries to inform creation of sustainability targets such as SBTi and corporate reporting on environmental impacts
  • How organizations disaggregate planetary boundaries to relevant temporal and spatial scales to inform appropriate action for sustainability
  • How organizations use the planetary boundary framework to shape sectoral and cross-sector collaborations
  • How organizations leverage planetary boundaries as a way to 'unlock' the complexity of the natural environment for business model innovation and/or product design
  • How Organizations Can Operate and Manage within Individual Planetary Boundaries
  • How organizations detect, interpret, and act when a planetary boundary is being approached or transgressed
  • How organizations prepare for risks associated with transgressing the boundaries and innovate to limit planetary boundary transgression
  • How organizations use planetary boundaries for constraint-driven innovation for enhanced practices, processes, business models, and/or collaborations
  • Which processes and practices enable firms to develop proactive and responsive strategies for long-term engagement with a specific planetary boundary
  • How organizations should balance trade-offs between proactive and responsive strategies for a given planetary boundary, given their industry and operating context
  • What roles different stakeholders play in shaping organizational responses to planetary boundary transgressions
  • How organizations can engage with least-studied boundaries such as ocean acidification, biogeochemical flows, atmospheric aerosol loading, stratospheric ozone depletion, and novel entities
  • How to Navigate Interconnections among Planetary Boundaries and with Social Foundations
  • How organizations adapt and innovate strategies, practices, and processes to address interconnections among multiple planetary boundaries
  • How efforts to stay within planetary boundaries can be aligned with advancing key social foundations and UN Sustainable Development Goals
  • How organizations can apply systems-thinking lenses to manage non-linear change, ecosystem risks, and feedback loops across planetary boundaries and/or social systems
  • What governance mechanisms, decision tools, or collaborative arrangements enable organizations and industries to navigate and manage trade-offs across boundaries
  • What role could concepts such as degrowth, carrying capacity, or post-growth business models play in helping organizations remain within interconnected ecological limits
  • How to Develop Alternative Organizational Theories and Practices from Planetary Boundary Biophysical Foundations
  • What innovations in practices, products, and business models emerge when organizational thinking begins with planetary boundaries
  • How integrating the planetary boundary framework can inform or reshape core organizational theories
  • How the planetary boundary framework can inform theory on crisis management and responding to ecosystem shocks such as natural disasters
  • How the planetary boundary framework might advance perspectives on desirable or alternative futures
  • What alternative forms of organizing can be theorized by taking planetary boundaries as foundational
  • How theory on circular and regenerative systems can be informed by considering planetary boundaries

Timeline

  • March 1, 2027: Full manuscript submission deadline

Associate editors

  • Gail Whiteman, University of Exeter Business School

item.title: Imagining Post-Growth
item.content:encoded:
Fred Basso, London School of Economics and Political Science

Nil Özçağlar-Toulouse, Université de Lille

Julien Troiville, ESG Université du Québec À Montréal

Humanity has entered a critical period to limit catastrophic climate change. Global warming is primarily due to human activity, and efforts to remain below 1.5°C have been insufficient. More than ever, marketing must act to encourage behaviors and choices compatible with truly sustainable lifestyles. Post-growth has emerged as a major research topic, carried by environmental and economic sciences as well as social sciences such as history, sociology and political science. It challenges the dependence of our societies on economic growth, the central place accorded to consumption-based well-being, and the supposed link between prosperity and productivism.

Interest in post-growth is reflected in the proliferation of articles in renowned scientific journals, the release of documentaries, and the creation of research centers dedicated to this topic. Management sciences are also engaged, as evidenced by calls for contributions for special issues devoted to post-growth or edited works. This special issue aims to advance theory and practice by exploring how researchers, consumers and practitioners implement strategies to prepare for post-growth.

This special issue welcomes empirical and conceptual contributions addressing post-growth in marketing from various theoretical, methodological and disciplinary angles (economics, psychology, history, law...), as well as research in non-WEIRD contexts and with indigenous and decolonial perspectives. In accordance with the principles of 'sobriety in research' and open science, particular attention will be given to proposals based on open data, panel data, and similar sources. In spring, a writing workshop in format will be organized and details will be communicated through various channels.

Potential topics

  • How marketing can challenge the status quo: Creating new desires vs. responding to individual needs; Marketing as a political choice reinforcing capitalism; Critical reflection on critical marketing; Ethical marketing practices and their relationship to the economic system; Individual vs. systemic responsibility in consumer behavior (I-frame vs. S-frame); Nudging and boosting as neoliberal strategies
  • How marketing can engage in degrowth practices: Transformative practices for degrowth strategies; Role of marketing experts in post-growth economic transitions; Reinventing marketing practices, training and education; Overcoming tensions within the economy; Internal growth transformations and moving away from materialism; Conceptual clarification of degrowth, post-growth, demarketing, regenerative economy, donut economy, ecosocial marketing, decarbonized marketing
  • How a post-growth economy can be sustained: Transitioning from unlimited desires to meeting human needs; Consumption corridors and sufficient consumption; Marketing roles and practices to maintain in post-growth society; Reduced working time and prefigurative organizations; Moving beyond technological utopias to social utopias; Public policies for degrowth transitions; Economic development equity between Global North and South; Escaping extractivism and postcolonial systems

Timeline

  • Invalid DateTime: Submission platform opens
  • Invalid DateTime: Special issue publication online
  • January 15, 2027: Full paper submission deadline

item.title: The Science of Group Meetings
item.content:encoded:
Joseph A. Allen, University of Utah

Nale Lehmann-Willenbrock, University of Hamburg

Meetings remain one of the most pervasive features of organizational life, serving as a critical venue for communication, collaboration, decision-making, and sensemaking in groups and teams. Yet, despite their ubiquity, meetings continue to spark debate over their effectiveness, efficiency, and impact on individuals, teams, and organizations. Moreover, the nature of group and team meetings in organizations is subject to ongoing change, with respect to meeting formats, purposes, and functions.

The aim of this Special Issue is to move forward and examine new perspectives on meetings in contemporary organizational life. We are interested in interdisciplinary and cross-disciplinary submissions that advance the meeting science literature, with a focus on empirical insights into group and team meetings. Both field studies and laboratory research methodology can contribute such insights. However, no studies based on individual-level, self-report, cross-sectional data unless substantiated by additional data will be considered.

Potential topics

  • Advances in meeting design and structuration in face-to-face, virtual, or hybrid group meetings
  • Effective meeting leadership and facilitation in various meeting formats
  • Psychological safety, inclusion, and equity in meetings
  • Meeting participation and engagement (including "pretend participation" or the act of appearing to participate in a meeting without actually contributing meaningfully to the group's goals)
  • Pre-meeting and post-meeting tasks
  • Decision-making and problem-solving in meetings
  • Linking within-meeting dynamics to relevant meeting experiences at the individual and/or team level (e.g., satisfaction, effectiveness, well-being, creativity)
  • Technology and meetings (e.g., AI applications in hybrid and virtual formats)
  • Meeting overload, fatigue, and recovery
  • Emotional dynamics and surface/deep acting in meetings
  • Diversity, identity, and power in meeting interactions
  • Training and interventions for effective meetings
  • Measurement and assessment of meeting quality and effectiveness

Timeline

  • October 1, 2026: Full papers submission deadline

item.title: Strategy and Aesthetics
item.content:encoded:
René Wiedner, Warwick Business School

Jennifer Whyte, University of Sydney

Saku Mantere, McGill University

Robin Holt, University of Bristol

Marie-Léandre Gomez, ESSEC Business School

There is broad recognition that organizational life cannot be fully understood or managed through rationalist frameworks. Scholars across the social sciences, including human geography and cultural theory, have long acknowledged how sensory experience, emotion, affect and embodied practice shape organization. Strategy studies are also beginning to understand how strategically significant phenomena–organizational routines, capabilities and identity, investment allocation and judgment, leadership, environmental adaptation–refuse to be confined to, and by, rational, logically structured analyses.

There is an aesthetic aspect to all strategy–it is as much vision as it reason; as much inspiration as analysis. Emotions, feelings, intuitions, desires and instincts can all have strategically significant influence. The symbolic and material dimensions of organising, alongside questions of purpose and structure across multiple human practices and fields, are all factors for which a successful strategic design must take account. The discursive, ecological and commercial forces to which organizations are adapting continually are encountered in aesthetic terms.

Organization theory is responding to this realization across multiple converging developments: the rise of design thinking and innovation discourse that foregrounds creative and experiential dimensions of value creation; growing attention to materiality and the physical environments in which work unfolds; and post-representational approaches that emphasize how knowing and organizing occur through sensory engagement rather than abstract cognition. From studies of organizational atmospheres and architectural spaces to analyses of craft work, branding practices, and the aesthetics of routine organizational artifacts, this scholarship has illuminated how aesthetic dimensions permeate organizational phenomena that were previously understood primarily through functional or instrumental lenses.

Despite this flourishing interest, explicit engagement with aesthetics in relation to strategy and strategic management has, for the most part, remained surprisingly limited. Aesthetically-minded scholars have examined topics adjacent to strategy, such as organizational identity, sensemaking, and innovation, with the strategic imperative toward creativity, or with questions of strategic fit and evolution. However, they have rarely focused explicitly on these being aesthetic considerations and experiences which are shaping the emergence and execution of organizational strategies. Conversely, mainstream strategy research has largely maintained its traditional emphasis on analytical frameworks, resource configurations, and performance metrics, with aesthetic dimensions remaining largely implicit or unexamined.

Contributing to this mutual neglect may be an underlying assumption that strategy and aesthetics are, to some degree, incompatible: strategy is typically associated with rational planning and directing, while aesthetic experiences are commonly viewed as detached from practical concerns. This special issue is dedicated to addressing this oversight, and to explicitly investigating the aesthetic aspects of strategic theory and practice. Strategy, we suggest, is grounded in aesthetics in a number of ways that merit further exploration.

Potential topics

  • The aesthetic qualities of strategy work: combining creative expression with analytical rigor; the coexistence of, and interplay between, poetics and reason
  • Aesthetically-infused experiences such as awe in understanding how strategic organizations resist the disenchantment of strategy work through over-rationalization
  • Studies of strategy confronting cultural landscapes encouraging the production and consumption of styles rather than goods, posing complex strategic identity choices across audiences with different stylistic preferences and evaluation criteria
  • How the strategic organization of affective forces is often caught in a fundamental ambiguity between instrumental organization and unmanageable reorganization of experience
  • Examinations of analogue and digital strategic devices and how these contribute to the performance of strategic styles, including strategy work in boardrooms and informal organizing contexts
  • Investigations of the strategic appropriation of artistic activity and how organizations draw from artistic practices to reinvent themselves and maximize profitability
  • Studies of organizational design and the formation of capabilities and identities that can be structured to elicit strategically significant commitments amongst stakeholders
  • Inquiries of processual forming and formation in strategy, invoking vitalist and new materialist philosophy and questions about organizational forms
  • Engagements with the raw material of strategy in formation, including how information and data have aesthetic forms and dimensions
  • Connecting strategy and temporality through aesthetics, including how strategy forms narrative plots that elicit specific feelings of progression, symbolic and communal attachments, and identities

Timeline

  • October 31, 2026: Manuscript submission window opens
  • December 1, 2026: Original manuscript submission deadline
  • April 1, 2027: Initial decision communication
  • August 1, 2027: Revise & resubmit deadline
  • December 1, 2027: Conditional acceptance decision communication
  • March 1, 2028: Iterations on conditional acceptances (with editors only)
  • May 1, 2028: Unconditional acceptance communication
  • November 1, 2028: Publication

item.title: Integrative Conceptual Reviews
item.content:encoded:
The Journal of Applied Psychology editorial team invites prospectus submissions that describe a proposed integrative conceptual review (ICR) manuscript on topic areas relevant to human resource management, industrial and organizational psychology, and organizational behavior.

An ICR article should be designed to synthesize relevant literature, identify significant knowledge gaps, highlight potential synergies between disconnected lines of research, extend theoretical development, and propose new directions for research.

Examples of the type of papers that are of interest include articles published in the Annual Review of Psychology, Psychological Science in the Public Interest, the Journal of Management review issue, the Academy of Management Annals, and top-tier handbooks.

An ICR prospectus can be submitted anytime via the Journal of Applied Psychology submission portal. A prospectus will be evaluated by the editorial team. Following review, the action editor will decide whether to invite a full submission, which will need to be responsive to issues raised during the initial prospectus review. Full papers should be submitted within 6 months of the invitation. The action editor and reviewers involved at inception will constitute the review team for full papers.

The prospectus should consist of: title and abstract (indicate Integrative Conceptual Review Prospectus at the top line of this page), with a transparency and openness statement as an author note on the title page that the TOP guidelines are not applicable to ICR proposals; summary (10 pages maximum, double spaced) that describes the contribution, structure, and coverage of the proposed paper; selected references (2 pages maximum); and tables or figures (2 pages maximum). The prospectus should provide a concise summary of the proposed paper that is sufficiently detailed to allow evaluation and should be prepared for blind review.

Evaluation criteria include: Relevance of the topic (topics should be meaningful and important); Coverage of the synthesis and review (reviews that are broadly integrative vs. narrow are more useful); Theoretical contribution (conceptual advances for building and extending theory are critical); and Research extension and novelty (the paper should clearly outline new lines of inquiry).

Potential topics

  • Human resource management
  • Industrial and organizational psychology
  • Organizational behavior
  • Literature synthesis and knowledge gap identification
  • Theoretical development and extension
  • New research directions

Timeline

  • Invalid DateTime: ICR prospectus submission deadline
  • February 18, 2027: Full paper submission deadline

item.title: Close Relationships in an Interdependent Social World
item.content:encoded:
Sandra Murray, University at Buffalo

Are close relationships in peril? Loneliness is increasing and markers of social engagement (e.g., marriage) are decreasing. This special section hopes to provide insight into this question by tackling the socially nested nature of interdependence itself.

Close relationships with significant others take place in the broader context of family responsibilities, such as those involved in parenting children and caring for aging parents; in the broader context of friendship networks, and broader communities; in the context of sociopolitical pressures, such as economic stress, racism, and political polarization; and in the context of technological changes, such as those posed by the insertion of AI into social life.

Potential topics

  • How contextual or socially nested nature of interdependence shapes close relationship dynamics
  • Relationship dynamics relevant to relationship initiation, maintenance, or dissolution
  • Close relationships in the broader context of family responsibilities (parenting children, caring for aging parents)
  • Close relationships in the broader context of friendship networks and communities
  • Close relationships in the context of sociopolitical pressures (economic stress, racism, political polarization)
  • Close relationships in the context of technological changes (AI insertion into social life)

Timeline

  • November 1, 2026: Submission deadline opens
  • January 31, 2027: Full paper submission deadline
