item.title: Reimagining Accounting for Inclusive Capitalism
item.content:encoded:
Charl de Villiers, University of Auckland

Ruth Dimes, The Open University

Anwar Halari, The Open University

Matteo Molinari, University of Bergamo

Capitalism remains the dominant framework for organising global economic life, yet its promises of prosperity and inclusion have increasingly come under scrutiny. Over the past few decades, the richest 1% have captured more than half of global wealth, while environmental degradation has accelerated at an alarming rate, threatening planetary boundaries. These outcomes have prompted growing calls for more inclusive and sustainable forms of capitalism, leading to the emergence of the concept of Inclusive Capitalism. Inclusive Capitalism seeks to reconcile profit-making with broader societal goals such as environmental stewardship, social justice and economic inclusion. However, its very emergence implies a failure of traditional neoliberal capitalism to deliver on its promises of inclusivity and prosperity. The push for Inclusive Capitalism thus reflects a growing recognition of capitalism's contradictions and the need to rethink how value is defined, measured and distributed.

Accounting is central to this rethinking, as it plays a central role in shaping capitalist systems. Financial accounting information serves as the backbone of capital markets, providing standardised, timely data that investors and other stakeholders rely on to evaluate firm performance and risk, and ultimately to determine share prices. Accounting defines what counts, what gets measured and what gets valued, and in doing so, it legitimises organisational behaviour. However, far from being a neutral technical practice, accounting reflects and reproduces the logics of capitalism. It privileges financial capital while marginalising other forms of value such as social, human, intellectual and natural capitals. Accounting practices are deeply embedded in power structures, legitimising the interests of some while silencing the interests of others.

Critical accounting scholarship has highlighted how accounting can both reproduce and challenge dominant logics and has attempted to theorise how the deep-seated structures underpinning accounting practices work. Scholars and practitioners have sought to imagine how accounting might steer capitalism to more inclusive ends. Developments such as ESG investing, impact investing, stakeholder capitalism, B-Corps and Circular Economy models offer new spaces for reimagining the role of accounting and accountants. More radical approaches such as counter-accounting initiatives and dialogic approaches have promoted participatory and inclusive forms of accountability through challenging capitalism's core logic. These initiatives highlight both the potential and limitations of accounting in supporting alternative forms of capitalism in an increasingly uncertain and polarised world.

This Special Issue invites contributions that critically and constructively examine how accounting may contribute to reimagining capitalism for a more inclusive future. We welcome interdisciplinary perspectives from accounting, finance, economics, law, sociology, political theory, linguistics, history, media studies, and natural sciences. Submissions may adopt critical, interpretive, or mainstream approaches, and may be theoretical, empirical, conceptual, or methodological in nature.

Potential topics

  • Historical and Conceptual Foundations: How has capitalism been historically conceptualised and what role has accounting played in shaping the boundaries of inclusion and exclusion in capitalist systems?
  • Accounting and the Language of Inclusion: How is capitalism linguistically constructed in corporate reports, policy documents, and the media? Why and how has the term 'capital' become associated more with financial capital than other forms of capital (natural, social, human, intellectual) and what are the implications of this? How do metaphors and anthropomorphic representations influence perceptions of accounting's role?
  • Accounting and Technology: How are emerging technologies shaping accounting practices that either widen or narrow inclusion? How might they entrench exclusion, concentrate power, or reinforce surveillance logics within capitalist systems? How is capitalism represented and contested in digital platforms and social media?
  • Critical Perspectives: How do accounting practices reflect and reproduce capitalist logics? What are the tensions between accountability, transparency, and inclusion in capitalist enterprises? Can alternative frameworks (e.g., feminist, indigenous, or social accounting) challenge dominant paradigms?
  • Institutional and Policy Dimensions: How can governments, regulators, and standard-setters use accounting to promote more inclusive and responsible capitalism? What are the implications of developments such as integrated reporting, sustainability standards, and ESG metrics?
  • Religion, Culture and Norms: How do religious organisations, cultural traditions and societal norms shape accounting practices and in what way do these practices create pathways that can support financial and social inclusion, or, conversely, undermine such goals?
  • Management Accounting Practices: How can management accounting systems incorporate multi-capital perspectives? What role do incentive structures and performance measurement play? How do managers change the way they think and act to reflect more integrated and inclusive ways of thinking about value creation?

Timeline

  • May 20, 2026: Abstract Deadline for Workshop
  • June 5, 2026: Notification of Acceptance for Workshop
  • July 7, 2026: Workshop date in Bergamo, Italy
  • November 1, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • January 31, 2027: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: Recherche quantitative inductive en GRH : enjeux et méthodes
item.content:encoded:
Clotilde Coron, Université Paris-Saclay

Data is increasingly recognized as a crucial resource for organizational innovation, with extensive and organized data exploitation considered a key driver of the ongoing fourth industrial revolution. HRM is not exempt from this trend, and the methodological challenges of leveraging increasingly diverse and massive datasets present significant stakes for both practitioners and academic researchers.

Recent reflections on applicable methods for extracting value from data often emphasize the disruptive potential of big data, presenting it as the foundation for a renewal of empiricism based on intensive exploration of data masses through exploratory methods, aimed at generating new knowledge through purely inductive logic. However, inductive, data-driven approaches remain rare in quantitative HRM studies, despite their capacity to transcend the classical dichotomy between qualitative/inductive and quantitative/deductive approaches in management sciences. Data-driven methodologies also help address criticisms leveled at hypothetico-deductive approaches, such as their strong standardization and difficulty in generating truly innovative theories.

This special issue aims to provide an updated overview of the challenges and opportunities of data-driven HRM, as well as inductive quantitative methods applicable in empirical research. Expected contributions may address these themes from methodological perspectives (such as presenting an innovative method with illustration in HRM), empirical perspectives (conducting a quantitative study on a subject by adopting an inductive approach), or conceptual perspectives (analyzing the stakes for HRM of data-driven management). Proposals presenting emerging or underutilized methods in francophone quantitative HRM studies will be particularly appreciated, including supervised learning, data mining, textual statistics, and longitudinal approaches.

Potential topics

  • Data-driven approaches in HRM
  • Inductive quantitative research methods
  • Big data exploitation and analysis
  • Supervised learning applications in HRM
  • Data mining techniques
  • Textual statistics
  • Longitudinal approaches
  • Innovative quantitative methods in HRM research
  • Theory building from data
  • Emerging methodologies in francophone HRM studies

item.title: Engagement et épreuves : l'expérience du travail dans les réformes en santé
item.content:encoded:
Nancy Côté, Université Laval

Jean-Louis Denis, University of Toronto

Henri Bergeron, Sciences Po

Tracey L. Adams, University of Western Ontario

Ce numéro spécial vise à interroger l'articulation entre la nécessité de réformer nos systèmes de santé et de services sociaux et les enjeux d'engagement et de mobilisation au travail que ces transformations soulèvent. Il s'inscrit dans une réflexion sur les façons de concilier la performance des systèmes de santé et le bien-être des personnes au travail.

Une approche critique des enjeux de mobilisation et d'engagement devient essentielle pour penser des politiques et des modes de gestion des ressources humaines plus novateurs et plus attentifs aux besoins et aux expériences des personnes au travail, et plus socialement légitimes, en intégrant les enjeux de justice organisationnelle, de conditions de travail et de voix des salariés, notamment à travers les relations avec les gestionnaires de proximité.

Souvent réduites à un enjeu de motivation au travail, ce numéro propose d'aborder la mobilisation et l'engagement comme des phénomènes profondément sociaux, situés à l'intersection des évolutions sociétales et des dynamiques propres au monde du travail. Cela conduit, au-delà des motivations individuelles, à s'intéresser aux contextes de travail dans lesquels les individus exercent leur métier ou leur profession, ainsi qu'aux environnements sociaux qui façonnent leurs statuts, les expériences du travail et les aspirations au travail.

Potential topics

  • L'articulation entre la nécessité de réformer les systèmes de santé et de services sociaux et les enjeux d'engagement et de mobilisation au travail
  • La conciliation entre la performance des systèmes de santé et le bien-être des personnes au travail
  • Les enjeux de justice organisationnelle et de conditions de travail
  • La voix des salariés et les relations avec les gestionnaires de proximité
  • La mobilisation et l'engagement comme phénomènes sociaux situés à l'intersection des évolutions sociétales et des dynamiques du travail
  • Les contextes de travail et les environnements sociaux qui façonnent les statuts et les expériences du travail
  • Les aspirations au travail et les politiques innovantes de gestion des ressources humaines

item.title: Cold Cases: Revisiting founding myths, iconic cases, and forgotten stories in management
item.content:encoded:
Anaïs Boutru, Université Paris-Dauphine, PSL

Linda Rouleau, HEC Montréal

Géraldine Schmidt, Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne

Albéric Tellier, Université Paris-Dauphine, PSL

Management research has long been populated by celebrated cases that have achieved the status of founding myths. Cases such as IBM's blindness to personal computing, Xerox's strategic myopia toward the graphical user interface, Nokia's fall to smartphones, the Mann Gulch fire, and Elton Mayo's Hawthorne experiments have become ubiquitous in the field's collective memory. These 'cold cases', endlessly cited and taught, structure ways of thinking and provide a shared foundation of representations that are central to the construction of epistemic communities.

Despite their pervasive influence, few studies scrutinize the empirical robustness, theoretical validity, or performativity of these emblematic cases. In management research, particularly in qualitative research, the risk of circularity is significant. Researchers working with inevitably heterogeneous and incomplete material may, even unconsciously, select data that confirm their theoretical priors, set aside disconfirming evidence, and ultimately favor demonstrations of the 'as if' type.

Management research's pursuit of 'theoretical gaps' has often privileged the production of new concepts at the expense of verification, reinterpretation, or falsification. This predilection leads to a stratification of knowledge where certain studies become canonical and generate 'halo effects', while others sink into oblivion not because they are invalid, but because they do not fit the dominant narratives of the discipline.

The aim of this special issue is to 'reopen the files of management' by challenging established truths, revisiting myths, excavating forgotten cases, and analyzing the processes of canonization and erasure that structure disciplinary memory. Famous cases such as Kodak, IBM, Enron, and Nokia must be regarded as epistemic artifacts, produced, reproduced, and sometimes distorted by scholarly communities, bearing narrative, moral, and institutional dimensions.

M@n@gement has established itself as a privileged venue for critical, reflexive, and interdisciplinary approaches in management research. This special issue continues this tradition by inviting the community to undertake an archaeology of its own knowledge. Revisiting 'cold cases' means interrogating how management research constructs its own history, its certainties, and its silences. It is a call to strengthen the cumulative and self-critical dimension of the field by restoring a rightful place to research grounded in the replication of experiments, the challenging of established findings, and recontextualization.

At a time when researchers are constantly pressured to produce 'new' knowledge, this special issue proposes to rehabilitate slow, reflexive research capable of revisiting taken-for-granted assumptions, reopening closed debates, and reinvigorating the controversies that are constitutive of knowledge production.

Potential topics

  • Reexamination and reinterpretation of canonical management cases (IBM, Xerox, Nokia, Kodak, Enron, etc.)
  • Empirical robustness and theoretical validity of emblematic cases in management scholarship
  • Performativity of famous cases and their role as epistemic artifacts
  • Processes of canonization and erasure in disciplinary memory
  • Circularity in qualitative management research and issues of confirmation bias
  • Role of founding myths in structuring management thinking and epistemic communities
  • Halo effects and the stratification of knowledge in management research
  • Forgotten cases and alternative narratives in management history
  • Critical reexamination of the Hawthorne experiments and other foundational studies
  • Replication, falsification, and verification in management research
  • Archaeology of management knowledge and disciplinary self-reflexivity

Timeline

  • October 14, 2026: Pre-submission workshop (online)
  • December 31, 2026: Full paper submission deadline

item.title: Social change, backlash, and resistance in organizations
item.content:encoded:
Sarah Richard, Audencia Business School

Lucie Noury, Audencia Business School

Pauline de Becdelièvre, Université Paris Saclay

Céline Louche, Waikato Management School—University of Waikato

Stéphan Pezé, Université Toulouse Capitole

The production and dissemination of knowledge, particularly on inequalities, climate change, and biodiversity, are increasingly under attack. These attacks are reflected in some political and administrative decisions adopted across several national contexts, such as the measures taken by President Donald Trump since his return to power. Beyond the US, academic freedom is being directly or indirectly undermined in many countries. For example, in France, controversies surrounding 'Islamo-leftism' within universities, reignited by the Minister of Higher Education, have been accompanied by concrete attacks on several scientific institutions.

Although research on grand challenges, sustainability, and ecosystem transitions is still ongoing, climate policies and the low-carbon transition are also under attack from many sides. These attacks range from climate scepticism to misinformation and lobbying, and aim to delay or weaken existing or future standards, as illustrated by the recent deregulation movement in Europe around the Omnibus law. Despite research pointing to the depletion of global resources, sustainable finance, ESG investing, and CSR are becoming increasingly polarized. Some asset managers are taking a more cautious approach to their commitments, and major players such as BlackRock announced in 2024 that they would be withdrawing ESG-labelled financial products. Some companies are reviewing their CSR practices and communication by adopting withdrawal or 'silence' strategies.

At the same time, the movement for equity, equality, and inclusion seems to be reaching a peak when it comes to considering diverse identities within organizations. And yet, it is simultaneously accompanied by growing opposition. The murder of George Floyd and the ensuing protests in 2020 intensified diversity initiatives, while fuelling a conservative backlash. In connection with these events, the public statements of certain companies, far from achieving consensus, have sometimes crystallized negative reactions.

Finally, the flexibilisation of work is also undergoing changes. While teleworking, part-time work and flexible hours have become the norm, particularly because of the health crisis, the ideal of constant availability remains dominant. Barriers to the use of these arrangements, such as stigmatization and career penalties, persist and are even becoming more pronounced, while calls for a return to the office are growing.

Whether it be attacks on science, the retreat from climate and financial commitments, the contestation of inclusion policies or the questioning of individualized management systems, these developments reflect a critical re-evaluation of social and ecological advances perceived as progressive: a phenomenon known as 'backlash'.

At its most basic level, backlash is defined as resistance to social progress. It is an active 'counterattack' against initiatives, programmes, knowledge, and policies that aim to change existing patterns of inequality and injustice. Used at a political level, the term refers to a retrograde goal of returning to a previous social condition, using extraordinary objectives and tactics that challenge dominant narratives to interfere with the dominant public discourse. The concept of 'backlash' emerged in the 1970s in the United States, in political science, to describe and analyse right-wing extremism. The emphasis is then placed on the link between 'backlash' and symbolic investment in the past: beyond simple opposition, backlash is often associated with fear of loss and nostalgia for an idealized past. In the 1990s, the feminist movement took up this notion, suggesting that every advance made by women triggers a hostile reaction to block or reverse their gains. Since then, it has been particularly mobilized in the field of gender studies and research on diversity, equality, and inclusion, which combine backlash with the study of the negative social and economic consequences affecting individuals who go against social norms.

Today, some researchers attribute a systematic nature to backlash. All projects aiming for social justice encounter resistance from privileged groups seeking to restore or maintain their power, contributing to a growing polarization of opinions. This development has been fuelled by several structural and psychological factors that have broadened its scope, including fear of losing resources, fear of the emergence of new dominant values, and questioning of existing values.

In management literature, the issue has mainly been explored from the perspective of diversity. Studies have focused on how women, particularly those in leadership positions, who challenge gender stereotypes may face a number of sanctions, such as hostile messages, negative evaluations, lack of promotion, or tensions with colleagues.

However, in a context where organizations play an increasingly political role, where they constitute a microcosm reflecting societal aspirations, and are part of increasingly connected networks of stakeholders, the phenomenon of backlash impacts organizations as a whole. Management and organization studies, together with other disciplines such as political science, sociology and psychology, can contribute to exploring the phenomenon at the institutional, organizational, managerial, and individual levels to shed new light on these dynamics, help us analyse them critically and position ourselves, as researchers and practitioners, in these debates.

At the institutional level, backlash can be understood through the three pillars—regulatory, normative, and cultural-cognitive—that structure the legitimacy of practices. It is not simply a matter of decline, but rather the outcome of institutional efforts aimed at undermining or redefining norms that were previously thought to be established. For example, the recent decline in commitment to sustainable development in the United States is based on anti-ESG laws passed in 37 states and decisions by the Supreme Court. At the same time, a 'backlash industry' is mobilizing framing marketing strategies to influence norms and representations. Nevertheless, institutional work does not only serve to destabilize institutions; it can also aim to defend, maintain, or strengthen them through various institutional maintenance practices involving stakeholders both inside and outside organizations.

At the organizational level, backlash can be overt, as illustrated by the explicit withdrawal of social or environmental policies under pressure following governance or political evolutions. These changes can generate opposition from stakeholders and can prove difficult to implement depending on how deeply rooted they are in regulations, culture, or processes. Alongside these apparent shifts, more subtle forms of backlash are also emerging: resource reductions, the withdrawal of objectives, silence, and changes in vocabulary, generating tensions between discourse and practice. Among stakeholders, trade unions play a central role in protecting existing rights. They constitute a counter-power that can either slow down backlash or contribute to it.

Managers appear to be key intermediaries, caught up in contexts of ambiguity, conflicting values and contradictory demands. Neither mere executors nor fully autonomous, they are faced with moral and political dilemmas, which sometimes lead them to support strategic changes, and sometimes to resist or attempt to preserve certain commitments. However, backlash remains poorly conceptualized as a specific managerial challenge with both organizational and societal dimensions.

At the individual level, organizational contexts characterized by normative uncertainty or contested values can exacerbate the identity and moral tensions experienced by individuals, with lasting effects on their commitment, well-being and career choices. These tensions drive action, with employees who are particularly sensitive to social or environmental issues making their voices heard within organizations in the form of internal activism. But threat is as much a cause as a consequence of backlash: it can emerge from perceived threats to the identity, status, or legitimacy of certain dominant groups, revealing ambivalent dynamics.

Taken together, these different levels do not function in isolation but feed into each other: institutional transformations redefine the organizational and managerial scope for action, which influences individual experiences, which in turn can help to consolidate, influence, or challenge existing institutional frameworks.

This special issue aims to contribute to the theorization of the backlash phenomenon by analysing its institutional, organizational, managerial, and individual manifestations. The objective is to gain a better understanding of the internal and external mechanisms that promote backlash, as well as its effects and their complex relationships. Ultimately, this special issue will seek to understand the representations and experiences of the various stakeholders faced with backlash, including the multiple forms of resistance it can generate.

This special issue calls for papers based on a variety of methodological and conceptual approaches and encourages the adoption of multidisciplinary approaches at the intersection of management science, sociology, political science, psychology, communication, philosophy and law, among others. Submitted articles may be conceptual or empirical and based on a variety of ontologies. They may explore in depth one of the manifestations of backlash (e.g. questioning of science, environmental commitments, DEI policies, or flexible work), take a more comprehensive approach to the phenomenon of backlash, or conduct comparative studies. Submitted manuscripts may also offer an analysis focused on a specific level of analysis (individual, managerial, organizational, or institutional) or undertake a multi-level analysis.

Potential topics

  • What are the different forms of backlash affecting organizations? Are there 'invisible' forms of backlash?
  • How and to what extent does backlash contribute to the deinstitutionalization of established norms (e.g. ESG, DEI, climate)?
  • What forms of institutional work produce or hinder backlash?
  • What roles do different modes of governance and different forms of organization play in weakening or, conversely, protecting social progress? Are democratic organizations, in particular, more or less prone to backlash?
  • How do organizations respond, resist, protect themselves, and participate in backlash?
  • What are the risks, uncertainties, and tensions generated by backlash? How can they be managed?
  • What forms of collective response are organized to face backlash (e.g. meta-organizations, networks, lobbying)?
  • How do individuals participate in or resist backlash (e.g. through employee activism)?
  • What is the impact of backlash on individuals (identity, career paths, values, social representations, experience)?
  • How does backlash transform or disrupt individuals' relationships with work and the company?
  • What forms of individual and collective resistance to backlash can be observed? What are the conditions and effects of this resistance?
  • What is the role of researchers and what stance should they adopt in response to this phenomenon?
  • What methodological and epistemological approaches are best suited to studying backlash, its mechanisms, and its consequences? What methodological innovations are needed to better understand its contemporary forms?
  • How can organizational theory contribute to understanding the phenomenon of backlash?
  • What are the multi-level interactions between societal, organizational, and individual backlash?
  • How can backlash contribute to the emergence of other backlashes?

Timeline

  • October 19, 2026: Deadline for paper proposals to workshop (maximum 3,000 words, including references)
  • November 19, 2026: Online paper development workshop organized by the guest editorial team across different time zones
  • February 1, 2027: Opening of submission period for full papers
  • June 1, 2027: Deadline for full paper submission
  • December 1, 2028: Publication date

item.title: Novel Forms and Models of Organization
item.content:encoded:
Masatoshi Kato, Kwansei Gakuin University

David Audretsch, Indiana University

Roy Thurik, Erasmus University Rotterdam

Maksim Belitski, University of Reading

Alex Coad, Waseda Business School

Eric Liguori, Florida State University

Rapid technological change, globalization of supply chains and demand, increasing physical and digital connectivity, and inter-dependencies between actors in innovation and entrepreneurial ecosystems are forcing entrepreneurs and managers to rethink how they organize beyond the manufacturing of products and services, how they innovate, what technologies they adopt, and what markets they enter. The forms and models of organization affect a firm's ability to become exceptional. At the core of firm organization, the factors that distinguish them from their counterparts in the industry and region are firm size, firm age, stage of entrepreneurial continuum, institutional context, and technology-savviness. Firms that have been able to optimize their organization will outperform their regional competitors, markets, and industry; create new forms of growth at a different pace; and approach the innovation and production frontier. Through organizations in different forms, entrepreneurs and mature firms create product and process innovation and coordinate people, external ecosystem actors, government, suppliers, and capital to achieve frontier outcomes.

This collection is especially interested in organizational forms enabling rapid growth without compromising productivity, efficiency, and societal impact, and facilitating innovation and market entry, firm resilience, and survival within both firm shocks and exogenous shocks. Moreover, the collection is interested in understanding how firms' high growth, scaling, and exceptional performance are driven by novel organizational forms. This focus is timely for the Journal of Small Business Management as an intellectual platform that studies why and how the most novel forms and models of organization in performance, growth, efficiency, and innovation are emerging in large tech firms and in exceptional performers among micro-, small-, and micro-firms, in social entrepreneurial firms, and even non-profit organizations. The special focus includes the novel forms of organization that allow for persistent steady growth, high value added, and other exceptional performers—such as niche innovators, scaleups, accelerators, blitzscalers, hidden champions, and Mittelstand-type firms and hyperspecialized firms—that repeatedly outperform their counterparts in the industry.

By combining specific forms of organization, these firms often operate nearby or at the innovation and production frontier despite constrained resources and through global or localized resource orchestration. Hidden champions or niche innovators—for example, hyperspecialized digital and non-digital firms that focus on a small set of activities and scale through digital technologies or localized networks and interdependencies with complements and partners often plugging into collaborators' value chains—are highly successful small firms that hold top global market positions in niche segments.

Global outreach is an important locus to understand novel forms of organization. Global firms, such as micro-multinationals or born-global firms, are young and small firms that internationalize early, working with a lean core and extensive external partners for production, distribution, or customer acquisition, and often relying on global value-chain orchestrators. While prior work has examined financial performance, resource management, scaling, and innovation in such firms, most evidence comes from European contexts, with little evidence from other regions of the world. For example, niche leaders in parts of Asia may begin with an imitation strategy and then move up the value ladder. These firms may be more likely to pursue listing and brand recognition, may expand into adjacent domains beyond niche focus, and may balance domestic and global knowledge via investment in training, R&D, and engagement with ecosystem actors regionally and globally. Little is known about how organizational forms differ across regions, industries, countries, and clusters, or which specific characteristics enable them to experiment, adopt, and develop certain forms of organization that ensure their exceptional performance.

This online collection invites work that theorizes and empirically examines novel forms and models of organization, including structures, processes, architectures, institutions, and governance, that enable firms of different ages, sizes, and niche focus to approach or redefine the productivity and innovation frontier. The collection welcomes research that opens the black box of novel forms and models of organization, enabling firms to outperform their close and distant competitors, recombine a variety of knowledge, and adopt new modes of working, hiring, and innovating to achieve exceptional performance. Additionally, the collection welcomes research that explains when, how, and why particular organizational forms and models outperform others across regions, industries, clusters, and ecosystems in diverse contexts of high-cost developed economies, high-cost emerging economies, and other developing economies.

This collection is expected to investigate how novel forms of organization can appear beyond the OECD and WEIRD countries representing Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic societies (primarily North America, Western Europe, Australia, and parts of East Asia like Japan/South Korea). Interestingly, most developed Asian economies have actively identified and cultivated niche leaders and innovators through national programs, such as Japan's Global Niche Top Companies Selection 100 and South Korea's World-Class 300 & Global Specialized Enterprise Cultivation. In China, two policy-driven categories—niche champions and specialized, advanced, differentiated, and innovative firms—aim to move small businesses up global value chains, emphasizing market performance, strategic uniqueness through innovation, competitive advantage, internationalization, and sustainable growth. Understanding new forms and models of organization for innovation and firm growth will create a rich empirical setting and extend existing growth and innovation theories.

Potential topics

  • How do firms adopting novel forms of organization differ in leadership, governance, and decision-making, and how do these differences shape innovation and productivity at the frontier?
  • What internal microstructures (e.g., boards, design, cross-functional teams, routines) enable firms to combine and recombine internal capabilities with external knowledge and ecosystem actors to achieve exceptional performance?
  • How do novel organizational forms affect authority, accountability, and coordination across functions, and what are the effects on innovation speed, product and managerial innovation, value creation, talent retention, growth, and scaling?
  • Which combinations of internal investment (make), external acquisition (buy), and alliance orchestration (ally) constitute novel organizational models that sustain frontier performance across firm types (hidden champions, niche leaders, sustained innovators, blitzscalers, scalers, etc.)?
  • How does the diversity (institutional and geographic) of external knowledge and innovation partners translate into firms adopting novel forms of organization, and what internal routines convert diverse inputs into outcomes?
  • Under what conditions do international vs regional knowledge collaboration and spillovers generate non-redundant knowledge that improves innovation and performance, and how do firms with different organizational forms apply, filter, and integrate this knowledge?
  • How does digitalization (AI and robotics, data systems, cloud, prominent role of intangibles, etc.) reshape internal process architectures, and which organizational forms best convert digital investments into productivity and innovation gains?
  • Which governance models (data rights, intellectual property, cybersecurity, partner contracts) enable novel organizational forms to adopt and scale complex technologies while maintaining trust and control in technology and partners?
  • How do digitally savvy firms pivot and reconfigure organizational forms to build resilience to supply, demand, and geopolitical shocks, and what design features predict faster recovery and sustained innovation?
  • How do firms implement novel forms of organization while embedded in industry and entrepreneurial ecosystems, and how does ecosystem position shape organizational models for innovation and scaling?
  • How do niche leaders and other exceptional performers orchestrate global supply chains as an organizational capability, not only a sourcing choice, across regional and international contexts?
  • What partner portfolio mixes (universities, suppliers, customers, competitors, government, research labs, conferences, competitions, trade and industrial associations, scientific communities) are associated with frontier outcomes, and what form of organization do firms need to adopt to efficiently govern such collaborations, knowledge spillovers, and firm strategies?
  • How do relationships with government shape novel organizational models through procurement, standards, subsidies, and cluster governance, and when do these relationships enhance versus constrain innovation and productivity?
  • How do organizational models vary between emerging and traditional industries and across industrial clusters of novel and emerging industries where traditional forms of organization are no longer working?
  • How do deglobalization pressures and techno-nationalism reshape firms' organizational choices?
  • What distinctive business model configurations characterize exceptional performers across countries, regions, industries, and stages of growth, age, and size, and how are these configurations enabled by organizational form?
  • How do European, Asian, American, and African leaders in WEIRD and non-WEIRD countries differ in adopting and experimenting with novel forms of organization?
  • What contextual factors explain these cross-country differences?
  • Do niche leaders exhibit distinctive innovation patterns (radical vs incremental, product vs process, ecosystem vs standalone), and which organizational designs best explain variation in these patterns and their performance effects?

Timeline

  • November 1, 2026: Manuscript submission opens
  • November 15, 2026: Submission deadline for extended abstracts and full papers
  • January 31, 2027: Manuscript deadline

item.title: Anti-Environmentalism and the Future of Green Growth
item.content:encoded:
Anastasios Xepapadeas, Athens University of Economics and Business

Simone Marsiglio, University of Pisa

Luca Gori, University of Pisa

In recent years, the global transition toward sustainable and low-carbon economic systems has encountered increasing political and social resistance. This phenomenon—broadly termed "anti-environmentalism"—encompasses a range of behaviors, beliefs, and policy stances that oppose or undermine environmental regulation, renewable energy expansion, and climate mitigation efforts. While green growth remains a central framework for reconciling economic development with ecological preservation, its implementation is increasingly conditioned by public acceptance, political will, and institutional credibility. Understanding how and why opposition to environmental policy arises—and how it interacts with economic incentives and policy design—is therefore a critical problem from both policy and academic perspectives.

It is therefore essential to examine the implications for pathways toward green growth and sustainable development when environmental considerations—particularly those related to climate change—are neglected under the influence of anti-environmentalist attitudes. This concern is made more urgent by scientific evidence indicating that climate change increases both the frequency and magnitude of extreme events, thereby amplifying expected damages. Moreover, the growing likelihood of transgressing critical planetary boundaries underscores the importance of understanding anti-environmentalist movements, which, if embedded in policy, could accelerate such boundary crossings. In addition, anti-environmentalist positions may hinder the mechanisms of creative destruction that facilitate transitions to low-carbon economies, offering a further area of relevance for the proposed Special Issue.

This Special Issue will bring together leading research in environmental economics, macroeconomics, political economy, and behavioral economics to explore the drivers, dynamics, and implications of anti-environmentalism for sustainable growth. It aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of how economic systems can maintain progress toward green growth amidst political polarization and societal backlash. We welcome a broad range of techniques and approaches, including optimal control, game theory, political economy, and network theory. Special attention will be given to methodological (theoretical, empirical or experimental) contributions aiming at disentangling the multifaceted nature of the anti-environmentalism and green growth relationship.

This Call for Papers is related to the HEDGE (Health, Environment, Development and Growth Economics) conference which will take place in Pisa on 5-7 February 2026, but it is open to everyone. Both conference participants and non-participants are encouraged to submit high-quality papers dealing with topics related to anti-environmentalism and green growth, broadly defined.

Potential topics

  • Economic, social and political determinants of anti-environmental attitudes and behavior
  • The impact of populism, misinformation, and lobbying on climate and environmental policy outcomes
  • Public perception and resistance to carbon taxation, green industrial policies, and regulation
  • Distributional and equity aspects of green growth as sources of policy backlash
  • The role of institutions and governance in shaping environmental resistance
  • International and comparative analyses of anti-environmental movements and climate cooperation
  • Behavioral and cultural dimensions of environmental skepticism and pro-growth narratives
  • Policy strategies for overcoming anti-environmentalist sentiment and fostering green, just and inclusive transitions
  • Economic growth under increasing climate-related extreme event risk, and the costs of climate skepticism

Timeline

  • March 31, 2027: Submission deadline

item.title: Wildfires in a Changing Climate: Impacts, Adaptation, and Policy
item.content:encoded:
Sarah Meier, ETH Zurich

Eric Strobl, University of Bern

Robert J. R. Elliott, University of Birmingham

In many regions of the world fire seasons have been lengthening, alongside increases in wildfire frequency and intensity. Climate change, shifts in land use, and the expansion of human settlements into fire-prone areas have transformed wildfires from largely localised hazards into systemic risks with cascading effects across ecosystems and economies. These developments have rendered many existing models, policies, and assumptions increasingly outdated, underscoring the urgent need for robust economic evidence to inform policy and private-sector decision making aligned with current and future wildfire conditions.

Wildfires and smoke pollution affect economies through multiple, interconnected channels. Beyond direct suppression costs and physical damages, wildfires disrupt production and supply chains, reduce labour productivity, influence tourism and recreation, and reshape migration and housing-market dynamics. Smoke exposure generates substantial public health burdens and impairs cognitive performance and labour market outcomes. These impacts occur within a context of rising public expenditures on prevention, suppression, and recovery, as well as rapidly evolving policy debates around insurance markets, land-use regulation, adaptation, and risk financing. Together, these dynamics highlight the need for empirical research that quantifies welfare consequences and evaluates the effectiveness of emerging policy responses.

Despite growing attention, many ecological and economic impacts of wildfires and smoke, particularly with regard to their persistence, remain under-studied, especially in regions that have not historically experienced large-scale wildfires but are now facing emerging risks. Cross-regional comparison can therefore support knowledge exchange between regions with long-standing fire experience and those facing emerging vulnerabilities, including across the Global North and South. At the same time, recent advances in data availability, remote sensing, and the use of AI-based technologies for monitoring, early warning, and suppression create new opportunities for applied research.

This Special Issue seeks contributions that advance empirical and policy-relevant understanding of wildfire impacts, as well as analyses that evaluate adaptation and management strategies aimed at reducing their welfare costs. We welcome applied research grounded in environmental, climate, and resource economics, including studies that use new data or innovative identification strategies to address this emerging challenge. Interdisciplinary work is encouraged where it strengthens economic insight into wildfire impacts and informs policy decisions.

Potential topics

  • Labour productivity, sectoral employment shifts, and worker mobility
  • Housing markets, mortgage risk, and migration and other behavioural responses to wildfire risk and exposure
  • Natural capital and ecosystem service valuation, including impacts on biodiversity, recreation, and forest asset pricing
  • Inequality, information access, and distributional impacts of exposure and monitoring technologies
  • Public finance, insurance markets, and the fiscal consequences for local and regional governments
  • Institutions, governance, and risk-sharing arrangements, including coordination across jurisdictions, public-private roles, and firm responses to wildfire risk
  • Prevention, suppression, and adaptation strategies, including land-use planning, prescribed burning, indigenous fire stewardship, and advanced monitoring and management technologies
  • Welfare losses from smoke exposure, including physical and mental health outcomes and associated human capital effects

Timeline

  • September 30, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: Valuing health and longevity: Advances and innovations
item.content:encoded:
Lisa A. Robinson, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

Olof Bystrom, OECD

Ståle Navrud, Norwegian University of Life Sciences

Mortality risk reductions typically dominate the benefits estimates for environmental policies. Recent reviews and syntheses of the value per statistical life (VSL) literature suggest that, while the research base is relatively strong for some settings, it contains significant gaps and inconsistencies. These include the need for more research on how attributes of the population and the risk affect these values. Deciding how to best synthesize and apply the estimates is also challenging.

The value of nonfatal risk reductions receives substantially less attention, although the expected reduction in cases of nonfatal illnesses or injuries associated with environmental policies is frequently large. As is the case for mortality risks, estimates of individual willingness to pay (WTP) are the preferred measure of values. However, due to gaps in the research literature, these risks are often valued using proxies such as averted costs.

Current approaches to valuation also raise a number of questions such as how to appropriately combine values for co-occurring effects and how to address distributional equity. Recent and emerging research addresses all of these problems, including new best practice WTP studies for mortality and morbidity, improved approaches for combining results across studies and transferring the estimates to different contexts, and innovations to address related challenges.

This special issue will highlight important contributions to this work and provide a useful reference for those interested in applying or building upon the results.

Potential topics

  • Value per statistical life (VSL) and population attributes affecting mortality risk valuations
  • Valuation of nonfatal risk reductions and morbidity using willingness to pay approaches
  • Synthesis and application of health valuation estimates across different contexts
  • Addressing co-occurring effects and distributional equity in health valuations
  • Benefit transfer methods and meta-analysis approaches for health valuation
  • Best practice willingness to pay studies for mortality and morbidity risk reductions
  • Combining and transferring valuation estimates to different policy contexts
  • Methodological innovations in environmental health economic evaluation

Timeline

  • October 31, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: Behavioural Environmental Economics & Policy (BEEP): trends and reflections
item.content:encoded:
Sanchayan Banerjee, King's College London

Lory Barile, University of Warwick

Traditional environmental economics addresses market failures (e.g., externalities, public goods, asymmetric information), using regulation and price-based instruments under a rational choice benchmark. Decades of evidence on bounded rationality, bounded self-interest, and bounded willpower reveal systematic departures from that benchmark, generating behavioural failures that can blunt or distort policy. These departures are well documented across core domains (e.g., environmental valuation, discounting of future outcomes and assets, and utility maximisation) and have given rise to a vibrant subfield: Behavioural Environmental Economics & Policy (BEEP).

This Special Issue will consolidate and showcase new contributions and evidence on how behavioural insights improve the design, delivery, and evaluation of environmental policy. Although BEEP has grown substantially, few efforts have mapped its diverse applications. We aim to fill this gap by providing theoretical, actionable, and evidence-based guidance for researchers and practitioners on putting BEEP into practice. Framed this way, the Special Issue will serve as a practical reference, grounded in recent cases that show why recognising and addressing human behaviour (and its failures) is essential to tackling urgent challenges, from climate change and biodiversity loss to air and water pollution.

We welcome conceptual/theoretical, empirical, and policy-oriented submissions that apply behavioural insights to understand, explain, or solve environmental problems. We particularly encourage quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-method designs (e.g., field/lab experiments, quasi-/natural experiments, RCTs, process evaluations), though literature reviews and theoretical contributions will also be considered. Overall, we seek contributions that diagnose and integrate market and behavioural failures and that design, test, and evaluate policies, including 'green nudges', that are both effective and welfare-enhancing.

Potential topics

  • Interactions between market failures and behavioural failures in environmental settings
  • Policy design that combines prices/standards with behavioural tools (defaults, salience/framing, simplification, commitment)
  • Welfare analysis (including psychological costs), ethics, and paternalism in environmental policy
  • Empirical identification of behavioural mechanisms; field/lab/quasi-experimental evidence
  • Heterogeneity, equity, and distributional consequences of behavioural environmental policies
  • Replication, meta-analysis, and open-science practices in this domain
  • Choice architecture and environmental outcomes
  • Interactions between behavioural instruments and prices/regulation
  • Welfare measurement and persistence (including psychological costs)
  • Distributional and equity dimensions
  • Climate cognition and communication
  • Evaluation and methods

Timeline

  • November 30, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: Technology Transfer through Collaboration: Bridging Academia, Policy, and Practice
item.content:encoded:
Maksim Belitski, Loyola University New Orleans

James Cunningham, Newcastle University

Riccardo Fini, University of Bologna

Simon Mosey, University of Nottingham

Phillip Phan, Johns Hopkins University

The Journal of Technology Transfer is pleased to introduce a new Special Collection on Technology Transfer through Collaboration: Bridging Academia, Policy, and Practice. The collection invites submissions that examine technology transfer, entrepreneurship, and innovation through collaborations between academic researchers and non-academic actors in policy and practice.

Timely and high-quality research on technology transfer often emerges from close interaction between academics, practitioners, and policymakers. Such collaborations can provide access to emerging phenomena, reveal underexplored mechanisms, and generate insights that may not be visible through conventional data sources or established theoretical lenses alone. The aim of this Special Collection is to support rigorous research that draws on boundary-spanning collaborations to advance scholarship on technology transfer while also generating meaningful implications for policy and practice.

The Special Collection particularly welcomes papers co-authored by academics and non-academic actors, including but not limited to technology transfer professionals, policymakers, entrepreneurs, innovators, investors, industry experts, platform managers, R&D managers, and innovation intermediaries. Such collaborations provide unique insights to policy and practice environments, enhance access to data, expand the contextual reach of empirical work, and address fundamental questions through a diversity of collaborative perspectives. Submissions should use collaborative engagement to develop new theory, enrich empirical analysis, access distinctive data, and address important questions in technology transfer, entrepreneurship, and innovation. Contributions should combine methodological rigor with practical and policy-relevant insight and demonstrate novel, impactful contributions to technology transfer scholarship.

The Special Collection is intended to create a lasting foundation for cumulative scholarly development rather than a one-off set of papers. The Journal of Technology Transfer remains firmly committed to its identity as a double-blind, rigorously peer-reviewed academic journal. Submissions must meet the journal's standards for theoretical contribution, methodological rigor, empirical credibility, and clarity of argument. The goal of this Special Collection is not to relax scholarly standards, but to broaden the range of relevant questions, data sources, contexts, and perspectives that inform high-quality research in technology transfer.

Potential topics

  • Papers co-authored by academics and non-academic actors, including technology transfer professionals, policymakers, entrepreneurs, innovators, investors, industry experts, platform managers, R&D managers, and innovation intermediaries
  • Technology transfer, entrepreneurship, and innovation through boundary-spanning collaborations
  • Development of new theory through collaborative engagement
  • Enrichment of empirical analysis using collaborative perspectives
  • Access to distinctive data through academic-non-academic partnerships
  • Addressing important questions in technology transfer, entrepreneurship, and innovation from multiple collaborative perspectives

item.title: Entrepreneurship and the Creation of Decent Work for All
item.content:encoded:
Societal changes, environment, political and financial crises inevitably affect labor markets and the quality of employment. Recent pandemic and global political changes have only demonstrated how quickly one's employment and workplace situation can change. Among other factors, entrepreneurship could play a crucial role in the creation of decent work, especially in a volatile environment.

Understanding the relationship between entrepreneurship and working conditions is crucial for supporting policies and instruments which aim at more productive, decent work, fair wages, better access to the labor market, and improved job opportunities for all.

In order to fully represent this multifaceted topic, we would like to gather a spectrum of current perspectives in a single Collection, facilitating a better understanding of possibilities and ways of striving toward the goal of 'achieving full and productive employment and decent work for all' (SDG 8 of the U.N.).

Submissions to this collection may be research or review articles, depending on the individual journal guidelines. Each submission will undergo thorough and rigorous peer review in accordance with each journal's peer review editorial policy. Accepted articles will be published in the journal they were submitted to, as well as highlighted on this collection page.

Potential topics

  • Equal pay for work of equal value
  • Gender discrimination in employment
  • Immigration and employment
  • Labor shortages after COVID-19
  • Modern slavery and child labor
  • Labor policy
  • Entrepreneurial enterprises, SMEs, and family businesses
  • Global entrepreneurial firms: organization design, emerging conceptions in entrepreneurship (i.e. born globals), globalization's challenges and opportunities, cultural differences
  • Remote work
  • Opportunity entrepreneurship as a direct way to generate high quality employment
  • Measuring and dealing with positive and negative externalities of new businesses

item.title: Building Digital Capabilities for Improved ESG Performance of Entrepreneurial Firms: Strategies for Tackling Challenges and Capitalizing on Opportunities
item.content:encoded:
Stefano Bresciani, University of Torino

Jawad Abbas, James Cook University

Fauzia Jabeen, Abu Dhabi University

In today's dynamic evolving technology landscape, firms face a transformative wave caused by technological advancements which are omnipresent, from automating manufacturing processes to leveraging big data analytics for strategic decisions. This development warrants entrepreneurial firms to develop digital capabilities strategically to navigate these changes, effectively positioning themselves for innovation and growth and enabling them to improve their Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance.

This call for papers focuses on exploring the strategies employed by entrepreneurial firms in building digital capabilities to enhance their ESG performance, addressing challenges, and leveraging opportunities in sustainable business practices.

In an ever-changing technological milieu where technological proficiency is synonymous with competitive advantage, fostering digital capabilities becomes a survival necessity, empowering firms to orchestrate agility, resilience, and sustainable performance. The digital age has ushered in transformative opportunities and challenges, redefining the landscape for entrepreneurial firms striving to align with ethical, social, and environmental responsibilities.

As mentioned in the aims and scope of the International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal, entrepreneurial ventures, characterized by innovation, agility, and risk-taking, are at the forefront of shaping the future of business. Their unique characteristics make them prime actors in navigating the complexities of integrating digital capabilities for improved ESG outcomes. Improving ESG performance is imperative for organizations, transcending mere compliance to embody a commitment to sustainable and ethical practices. This commitment holds profound implications for various stakeholders, ranging from shareholders to customers, suppliers, employees, and others. Improved ESG performance mitigates risks associated with environmental impact and social responsibility, enhances corporate reputation, and attracts conscientious investors. Stakeholders increasingly scrutinize ESG metrics as a reflection of an organization's ethical standing and long-term viability. It fosters a symbiotic relationship, aligning corporate objectives with societal expectations and contributing to building a more responsible and resilient business ecosystem.

This Collection aims to unravel the intricate role of building digital capabilities in entrepreneurial firms' improved ESG performance. By exploring this intersection, we seek to understand how digital capabilities can contribute to a more environmentally and socially responsible entrepreneurial firm with a strong governance structure. We invite experimental, conceptual, theoretical, and empirical studies exploring the convergence of digital capabilities in shaping entrepreneurial firms' ESG performance, shed light on challenges, and explain solutions.

While these topics and questions are our primary interests, we remain open to manuscripts that explain other complexities relevant to digital capabilities and ESG performance. We are keen to receive manuscripts that employ innovative methods and engage deeply with the prevailing dilemmas and dialogues in entrepreneurial research. Your insights and academic rigor will help broaden our collective comprehension of the complexities, challenges, and impacts surrounding building digital capabilities strategies and their implications for ESG performance.

Potential topics

  • How do entrepreneurial ventures define and measure ESG performance in the digital era? And what critical digital capabilities contribute to their improved ESG performance?
  • What challenges do entrepreneurial firms face in integrating digital solutions to enhance environmental sustainability? What could be the best practices for tackling those challenges?
  • What are the possible learning mechanisms and knowledge-sharing processes within entrepreneurial ecosystems that could foster development of digital capabilities for ESG goals?
  • What roles do leadership and organizational culture play in fostering digital capabilities for superior ESG performance in entrepreneurial firms?
  • How can entrepreneurial firms effectively utilize digital technologies to measure and improve their environmental performance within ESG frameworks?
  • How can digital capabilities be harnessed to address diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) challenges in entrepreneurial firms, contributing to improved social sustainability?
  • How do digitalization efforts impact the governance structures of entrepreneurial firms in the context of sustainability? What actions could be taken to improve it?
  • To what extent do regulatory frameworks influence the adoption of digital strategies for ESG compliance in entrepreneurial settings?
  • How do digital technologies facilitate transparency and accountability in ESG reporting for entrepreneurial firms?
  • How can entrepreneurial firms balance profitability goals with sustainable practices through digital transformations? Under this scenario, which opportunities and challenges could arise?
  • What lessons can we learn from recent, real-world cases that showcase the impact of digital capabilities on ESG performance in different industries, particularly entrepreneurial firms, and how can new guidelines lead toward improved ESG performance?

item.title: Bibliometric Measures of Epistemic Change
item.content:encoded:
Bibliometrics has a long-standing interest in tracing epistemic change. The question of how epistemic change is reflected in publications is implicit to evaluative bibliometrics because the quality of a paper is measured through its impact, which can be understood as the extent to which a paper changes later research. Beyond this idea underlying bibliometric assessments, the question of how to identify and trace emerging fields or emerging technologies has attracted considerable attention, and the dynamics of topics has been traced with bibliometric methods. These approaches either identify emerging topics and technologies by searching for rapidly growing clusters of publication or trace changes that are known to exist and trace them using citation patterns, keywords or combinations thereof. The current interest in the identification of exceptional papers reflects a similar interest in epistemic change.

The application of bibliometric methods for tracing epistemic change also appears to be hindered by constraints that are not necessary but appear to be somewhat self-inflicted in that they are due to methodological traditions that are taken for granted in bibliometrics. Recent indicators like Innovativeness, Novelty, Originality or Disruptiveness describe single papers and attempt to codify the epistemic change they bring about. This design is based on three implicit assumptions. First, the construction of indicators of epistemic change from metadata of individual papers implies the assumption that the epistemic change is an event rather than a process. Second, the construction of these indicators assumes that the event that is measured by the indicator is fully reported in exactly one paper. Third, indicators sacrifice specificity for comparability, attempting to describe how much epistemic change is represented by a paper while being unable to report the kind of change that has occurred.

These three limitations appear to be the results of choices made by indicator designers rather than fundamental limitations of bibliometrics, and come on top of the only truly fundamental limitation: the dependence of bibliometrics on the signal about a publication's content that is contained by the publication's metadata. This limitation raises a fundamental question about the validity of bibliometric measures of epistemic change. Since we don't know how the content of a paper is reflected in bibliometric metadata, we cannot assess the content or strength of the signal metadata contain and thus cannot know if the signal is validly codified by an indicator.

The special collection presents papers that were developed in a series of workshops which addressed these four challenges, providing perspectives on conceptualisation and operationalisation of epistemic change, construction of ground truths, analysis of metadata content, validation of indicators, and application of artificial intelligence methods to publications.

Potential topics

  • Conceptualisation and operationalisation of epistemic change for bibliometric tracing
  • Construction of ground truths for development and testing of bibliometric methods
  • Metadata content related to epistemic change in bibliographic records
  • Validation of established bibliometric indicators against ground truths
  • Application of large language models to full texts for identifying epistemic change

Timeline

  • October 31, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: International Business in a Reconfiguring Southeast Asia
item.content:encoded:
S. Tamer Cavusgil, Georgia State University

Marleen Dieleman, IMD Business School

Md. Tareq Hossain, Thammasat University

Ruey-Jer Bryan Jean, National Taiwan University

Destan Kandemir, Georgia State University

Suntichai Kotcharin, Thammasat University

Hussain Rammal, Adelaide University

Southeast Asia has emerged as one of the most consequential yet under-theorized regions in contemporary international business. The ten ASEAN economies collectively form the world's fifth-largest economic bloc, attracted record FDI inflows of approximately US$ 230 billion in 2023 and 2024, and are projected to add roughly 140 million new consumers by 2030. The region has become a critical site for phenomena that strain or extend prevailing IB theory: it is simultaneously a primary beneficiary of China-plus-one supply chain reconfiguration, a launchpad for a new generation of regional multinationals, and a laboratory for institutional heterogeneity, where ten countries with widely divergent political systems, regulatory regimes, religious traditions, and stages of development cooperate without monetary union or labor mobility.

Despite this empirical importance, Southeast Asia remains underrepresented in top international management journals, where research on emerging Asia continues to be dominated by Chinese and Indian contexts and where the theoretical voice of scholars based in the region itself is frequently filtered through Western co-authorship and Western analytical frames. This Focused Issue invites contributions that take Southeast Asian phenomena as theoretically generative rather than merely empirically illustrative, and actively encourages submissions led by scholars based in the region. The issue aims to advance international management theory beyond the BRICS-centric vocabulary that has shaped emerging-market IB research, and to surface concepts, mechanisms, and boundary conditions that the region's distinctive configuration of family capitalism, ethnic-Chinese business networks, state-linked enterprises, hyper-digital consumer markets, and ASEAN-level institutional layering uniquely reveals.

Potential topics

  • The Rise and Internationalization of Southeast Asian Multinationals - Theory-building work on springboard, asset-augmentation, and catch-up strategies of ASEAN-origin MNEs; internationalization trajectories compared to Chinese and Indian counterparts; asset-augmentation versus ownership-advantage-based theories of FDI; platform architecture in cross-border expansion of digital-native champions; internationalization of state-linked enterprises under dual commercial and political principals
  • Supply-Chain Reconfiguration, Maritime Connectivity, and Regional Supply-Chain Governance - Integration of Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Philippines into reorganized global value chains; upgrading dynamics and co-location strategies with Chinese MNEs; port competitiveness and hinterland connectivity; maritime logistics resilience; multimodal transport-corridor integration; dual-sourcing and supply-chain resilience strategies; digital logistics platforms; ASEAN's role in global production-network reconfiguration
  • Cross-Border Trade, Geopolitics, and the Middle-Power Firm - How Southeast Asian firms hedge between US, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and European spheres of influence; non-market strategy under strategic ambiguity; role of Singapore as neutral coordination hub; strategic ambiguity and hedging among ASEAN-based firms; locational advantages of neutral coordination hubs; non-market strategy navigating US-China technology restrictions; implications of middle-power diplomacy for firm internationalization
  • Indigenous Theorizing and Methodological Innovation from the Region - Submissions drawing on Southeast Asian intellectual traditions, languages, or fieldwork methods; indigenous concepts such as gotong royong, kreng jai, and bayanihan as theoretical resources; multi-language qualitative research designs and epistemology of translation; postcolonial perspectives on knowledge production; methodological pluralism including ethnographic, historical-archival, and participatory approaches

item.title: Strategizing in a Fractured World: MNE Responses to Fragmented Stakeholder and Institutional Pressures
item.content:encoded:
Srividya Jandhyala, École Supérieure des Sciences Économiques et Commerciales

Vera Kunczer, Copenhagen Business School

Jonas Puck, Vienna University of Economics and Business

Harald Puhr, Universität Innsbruck

Michael Wolfesberger, Vienna University of Economics and Business

Firms and policymakers are struggling to address a seemingly 'perfect storm' of political, social and economic disruptions. Rising national security concerns, populist politics, and societal pressures have produced fragmentation, i.e., the coexistence of overlapping, conflicting, or weakly coordinated rules and pressures across national, supranational, and societal spheres. MNEs must navigate the triality of home, host, and supranational institutions in cross-border business. For example, multilateral frameworks that could shape MNE sustainability initiatives, such as the UN SDGs and the Paris Agreement, face domestic resistance in some countries and are part of the legal basis in others. Such tensions between supranational frameworks and nationalist movements or policies can create conflicting institutional logics and institutional schisms. While international institutions shape firms' assessments of their domestic environments, in adapting to these fractured environments, MNEs may also amplify institutional pluralism through local responses.

In light of these contradictory institutional and stakeholder pressures, this focused issue seeks to advance understanding of how MNEs strategize in fractured environments and the resulting stakeholder pressures. Papers may address one of the proposed areas or other relevant areas related to MNE responses to fragmentation and stakeholder pressures. Interdisciplinary submissions that complement business perspectives with approaches from other disciplines, particularly political science, are welcome. Both conceptual and empirical papers (quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods) are welcome. The focused issue is open to contributions focused on methodological advances, theory testing, and theory development.

Potential topics

  • What drives the exposure of MNEs to institutional fragmentation and fracturing?
  • When and how do MNEs integrate market- and non-market strategies across global markets in response to fragmented stakeholder and institutional pressures?
  • How do MNEs manage and organize their response strategies across different markets?
  • How do institutional fragmentation and geopolitical tensions shape interactions within firms?

  • September 30, 2026: Submission deadline
